::: callout-note
## Design framing

The goal of this analysis is to characterize a **stable between-person climate-attitude system**, not wave-specific fluctuations. Repeated attitude items are therefore harmonized to a common 0–1 scale and later averaged across all available waves for each participant. The resulting participant-level scores are interpreted as typical positions in the climate-attitude field over the study period.

Wave-5 behavioral items are treated separately as downstream outcomes and are not averaged together with the repeated attitude variables.
:::

```{r availability-summary}
na_special <- function(x) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  dplyr::case_when(
    x %in% c(98, 99, -98, -99) ~ NA_real_,
    TRUE ~ x
  )
}

df_long_cov <- df_long |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    across(any_of(c(candidate_items_raw, beh_items)), na_special)
  )

availability_by_wave_all <- df_long_cov |>
  dplyr::group_by(wave) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    across(any_of(c(candidate_items_raw, beh_items)), ~ mean(!is.na(.x))),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    -wave,
    names_to  = "item",
    values_to = "prop_observed"
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(item_status, by = "item")

availability_summary <- availability_by_wave_all |>
  dplyr::group_by(item, status, reason) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    waves_available = sum(prop_observed > 0.05),
    first_wave_obs  = ifelse(any(prop_observed > 0.05),
                             min(wave[prop_observed > 0.05]), NA),
    last_wave_obs   = ifelse(any(prop_observed > 0.05),
                             max(wave[prop_observed > 0.05]), NA),
    waves_label     = ifelse(is.na(first_wave_obs), NA,
                             paste0(first_wave_obs, "–", last_wave_obs)),
    min_coverage    = round(min(prop_observed[prop_observed > 0]), 2),
    max_coverage    = round(max(prop_observed), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(
    factor(status, levels = c("screened", "dropped upfront")),
    desc(waves_available),
    item
  )

# skim variables
skimr::skim(df_long_cov |> dplyr::select(any_of(c(candidate_items_raw, beh_items))))
```

## 1.2 Wave coverage

```{r availability-plot, fig.height=10, fig.width=8}
item_order <- availability_summary |>
  dplyr::arrange(desc(waves_available), desc(max_coverage), item) |>
  dplyr::pull(item)

availability_by_wave_all |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    item = factor(item, levels = rev(item_order))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(wave), y = item, fill = prop_observed)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = ifelse(prop_observed > 0, scales::percent(prop_observed, accuracy = 1), "")),
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "grey95",
    high = "#2166ac",
    limits = c(0, 1),
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    name = "Observed"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  labs(
    title = "Item coverage across waves",
    subtitle = "Cell values show proportion observed in each wave",
    x = "Wave",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10)
  )
```

::: callout-note
The coverage plot shows how widely each candidate item was fielded across waves and how complete it was when fielded.

At this stage, the plot is used only to document temporal coverage and to justify a very limited upfront exclusion step. On coverage grounds alone, only the `ew3_*` items are removed before the main EDA because they are too sparse to be useful in repeated-attitude screening. All remaining repeated-attitude variables are carried into Section 3 and evaluated there.
:::

# 1.3 Data cleaning and rescaling

```{r cleaning-helpers}
rescale01 <- function(x, from) {
  (x - from[1]) / (from[2] - from[1])
}

# Recode 98, 99, -98, -99 to NA; coerce to numeric
na_special <- function(x) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  dplyr::case_when(
    x %in% c(98, 99, -98, -99) ~ NA_real_,
    TRUE ~ x
  )
}

# Recode binary 1/2 items to 0/1
recode_binary01 <- function(x) {
  x <- na_special(x)
  dplyr::case_when(
    x == 1 ~ 0,
    x == 2 ~ 1,
    TRUE   ~ NA_real_
  )
}

# cc1: handles 0/1/2 (No/DK/Yes) and 0/1/99 (No/Yes/DK) coding
recode_cc1_midpoint <- function(x) {
  x  <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  ux <- sort(unique(x[!is.na(x)]))

  if (all(ux %in% c(0, 1, 2))) {
    dplyr::case_when(
      x == 0 ~ 0,
      x == 1 ~ 0.5,
      x == 2 ~ 1,
      TRUE   ~ NA_real_
    )
  } else if (all(ux %in% c(0, 1, 99))) {
    dplyr::case_when(
      x == 0  ~ 0,
      x == 1  ~ 1,
      x == 99 ~ 0.5,
      TRUE    ~ NA_real_
    )
  } else {
    dplyr::case_when(
      x == 0  ~ 0,
      x == 1  ~ 0.5,
      x == 2  ~ 1,
      x == 99 ~ 0.5,
      TRUE    ~ NA_real_
    )
  }
}

recode_cc1_dropdk <- function(x) {
  x  <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  ux <- sort(unique(x[!is.na(x)]))

  if (all(ux %in% c(0, 1, 2))) {
    dplyr::case_when(
      x == 0 ~ 0,
      x == 2 ~ 1,
      TRUE   ~ NA_real_
    )
  } else {
    dplyr::case_when(
      x == 0 ~ 0,
      x == 1 ~ 1,
      TRUE   ~ NA_real_
    )
  }
}

# cc2 recode:
# 4 = climate change isn't happening -> 0
# 2 = natural causes               -> 1
# 3 = both equally                 -> 2
# 1 = human activities             -> 3
# then rescale to 0–1
recode_cc2_ord <- function(x) {
  x <- na_special(x)
  out <- dplyr::case_when(
    x == 4 ~ 0,
    x == 2 ~ 1,
    x == 3 ~ 2,
    x == 1 ~ 3,
    TRUE   ~ NA_real_
  )
  rescale01(out, from = c(0, 3))
}

mean_or_na <- function(x) {
  if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}
```

```{r clean-long-data}
df_long_h <- df_long |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cc1_raw = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(cc1)),
    cc1     = recode_cc1_midpoint(cc1),

    # core repeated items on a common 0–1 scale
    cc3     = rescale01(na_special(cc3), from = c(1, 4)),
    cc6     = rescale01(na_special(cc6), from = c(1, 4)),

    cc4_world    = rescale01(na_special(cc4_world),    from = c(1, 4)),
    cc4_wealthUS = rescale01(na_special(cc4_wealthUS), from = c(1, 4)),
    cc4_poorUS   = rescale01(na_special(cc4_poorUS),   from = c(1, 4)),
    cc4_comm     = rescale01(na_special(cc4_comm),     from = c(1, 4)),

    cc5_world    = rescale01(na_special(cc5_world),    from = c(1, 4)),
    cc5_wealthUS = rescale01(na_special(cc5_wealthUS), from = c(1, 4)),
    cc5_poorUS   = rescale01(na_special(cc5_poorUS),   from = c(1, 4)),
    cc5_comm     = rescale01(na_special(cc5_comm),     from = c(1, 4)),

    cc_pol_tax   = rescale01(na_special(cc_pol_tax), from = c(1, 5)),
    cc_pol_car   = rescale01(na_special(cc_pol_car), from = c(1, 5)),

    cvcc9_cc       = rescale01(na_special(cvcc9_cc), from = c(1, 5)),
    cvcc4_should   = rescale01(na_special(cvcc4_should), from = c(1, 5)),
    cvcc4_will     = rescale01(na_special(cvcc4_will), from = c(1, 5)),
    cvcc4_personal = rescale01(na_special(cvcc4_personal), from = c(1, 5)),
    cvcc_worryothers = rescale01(na_special(cvcc_worryothers), from = c(1, 4)),

    pol_ideology = rescale01(na_special(pol_ideology), from = c(1, 5)),
    ew5          = rescale01(na_special(ew5), from = c(1, 4)),
    ew6          = rescale01(na_special(ew6), from = c(1, 4)),

    # screening-only variables cleaned into analytically usable form
    cc2     = recode_cc2_ord(cc2),
    cvcc6   = rescale01(na_special(cvcc6), from = c(1, 5)),
    pol7    = recode_binary01(pol7),
    pol7_pi = recode_binary01(pol7_pi),
    cc10    = rescale01(na_special(cc10), from = c(1, 7)),
    cc11    = rescale01(na_special(cc11), from = c(1, 7)),
    cc12    = rescale01(na_special(cc12), from = c(1, 7))
  )
```

```{r clean-wave5-behavior}
df_w5_h <- df_w5 |>
  dplyr::mutate(across(any_of(beh_items),
                        ~rescale01(na_special(.x), from = c(1, 5))))
```

::: callout-note
All repeated-attitude variables entering the EDA are cleaned into analytically usable form before person-level averaging. Wherever possible, ordinal items are put on a common 0–1 scale so that participant-level averages are comparable across variables. Special missing-value codes are recoded to `NA`, and `cc1` is handled separately because its coding differs across waves and includes a “don’t know” category.

The variables that enter Section 3 are not yet being treated as final network nodes. This cleaning step is only meant to put them into a consistent form for empirical screening.

`cc2` is treated as a special case. The original item distinguishes “human activities,” “natural causes,” “both equally,” and “climate change isn’t happening.” For screening purposes, it is analytically recoded to an ordered 0–1 scale running from climate-change non-endorsement through natural and mixed attribution to explicit human-cause attribution (`not happening = 0`, `natural = 1`, `both = 2`, `human = 3`, then rescaled to 0–1). This recoding is used only for provisional inclusion in the empirical screening stage.
:::

# 2. Variable dictionary

This dictionary documents the repeated-attitude variables that enter the EDA screening stage, together with the wave-5 behavior items that are used later as downstream outcomes. At this point, the table is descriptive only: it records item content and response format, but does not yet determine which variables will survive into the final composite set.

## Repeated-attitude variables entering EDA screening

| item | domain | question description | response format | note |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| `cc1` | Belief | “Do you think global warming / climate change is happening?” | Yes / No / Don’t know | `cc1` is recoded separately because the “don’t know” category differs across waves |
| `cc2` | Attribution | “Do you think rising temperatures are a result of human activities, natural causes, both, or not happening?” | 4-category single response: Human activities / Natural causes / Both / Not happening | For screening, this is analytically recoded to an ordered 0–1 gradient from non-endorsement through natural and mixed attribution to explicit human attribution |
| `cc3` | Problem severity | “Would you say global warming / climate change is…” | 4-category single response: Not a problem / A minor problem / A serious problem but not a crisis / A significant crisis | Severity candidate with narrower temporal coverage |
| `cc6` | Concern / worry | “How worried are you about current and future global warming / climate change?” | 1 = not at all worried to 4 = very worried | Repeated concern item |
| `cc4_world` | Present harm | “How much, if at all, do you think global warming / climate change is currently harming the world in general?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Wave 1 includes `99 = don’t know` |
| `cc4_wealthUS` | Present harm | “How much, if at all, do you think global warming / climate change is currently harming wealthy communities within the United States?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Wave 1 includes `99 = don’t know` |
| `cc4_poorUS` | Present harm | “How much, if at all, do you think global warming / climate change is currently harming poor communities within the United States?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Wave 1 includes `99 = don’t know` |
| `cc4_comm` | Present harm | “How much, if at all, do you think global warming / climate change is currently harming your local community?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Wave 1 includes `99 = don’t know` |
| `cc5_world` | Future harm | “How much, if at all, do you think global warming / climate change will harm future generations of people in the world in general?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Wave 1 includes `99 = don’t know` |
| `cc5_wealthUS` | Future harm | “How much, if at all, do you think global warming / climate change will harm future generations of people in wealthy communities within the United States?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Wave 1 includes `99 = don’t know` |
| `cc5_poorUS` | Future harm | “How much, if at all, do you think global warming / climate change will harm future generations of people in poor communities within the United States?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Wave 1 includes `99 = don’t know` |
| `cc5_comm` | Future harm | “How much, if at all, do you think global warming / climate change will harm future generations of people in your local community?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Wave 1 includes `99 = don’t know` |
| `cc_pol_tax` | Policy support | “How much do you support or oppose… a tax or fee on the production or distribution of carbon-based fuels?” | 1 = strongly oppose to 5 = strongly support | Direct climate-policy item |
| `cc_pol_car` | Policy support | “How much do you support or oppose… stronger carbon emissions standards for car manufacturers?” | 1 = strongly oppose to 5 = strongly support | Direct climate-policy item |
| `cvcc9_cc` | Response orientation | “Scientists with the appropriate expertise should guide climate response.” | 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree | Expert-guidance / response-orientation item |
| `cvcc6` | Individual action | “Global warming / climate change requires each of us to act in order to help solve a serious social and environmental problem.” | 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree | Wording shifts somewhat across waves; included for EDA screening |
| `cvcc4_should` | Social norms | “People should permanently shift some lower-carbon behaviors following COVID.” | 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree | Injunctive-norm candidate |
| `cvcc4_will` | Norms | “People / most people will permanently shift some lower-carbon behaviors following COVID.” | 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree | Descriptive-norm candidate; codebook notes a wave-3 fix |
| `cvcc4_personal` | Personal intention | “I will permanently shift some lower-carbon behaviors following COVID.” | 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree | Personal-intention candidate |
| `cvcc_worryothers` | Perceived public worry | “How worried do you think most Americans are about global warming / climate change these days?” | 1 = not at all worried to 4 = very worried | Earlier waves use somewhat different public-worry wording; included for screening |
| `pol_ideology` | Politics | “What is your political ideology?” | 1 = very conservative to 5 = very liberal | Political self-placement |
| `pol7` | Politics / policy tradeoff | “Which statement comes closer to your views… stricter environmental laws hurt the economy, or stricter environmental laws are worth the cost?” | Binary single response | Political tradeoff candidate |
| `pol7_pi` | Perceived public politics | “Which statement do you think comes closer to the views of most Americans… stricter environmental laws hurt the economy, or are worth the cost?” | Binary single response | Perceived-public tradeoff candidate |
| `ew5` | Weather risk | “How worried are you about an extreme weather event or natural disaster happening to you personally in the next year?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Weather-risk item |
| `ew6` | Weather preparedness | “How much have you prepared for a future extreme weather event or natural disaster?” | 1 = not at all to 4 = a great deal | Weather-preparedness item |
| `cc10` | Risk perception | “To what extent are the risks of global warming / climate change known precisely by the people who are exposed to those risks?” | 1 = known precisely to 7 = unknown | Psychometric risk-perception candidate |
| `cc11` | Risk perception | “If you are exposed to the risks of global warming / climate change, to what extent can you, through your own actions, control whether you are harmed?” | 1 = personal risk can be controlled to 7 = personal risk can’t be controlled | Psychometric risk-perception candidate |
| `cc12` | Risk perception | “Is the risk of global warming / climate change a risk that people have learned to live with and can think about reasonably calmly, or is it a risk that people dread?” | 1 = calm to 7 = dread | Psychometric risk-perception candidate |

## Wave-5 downstream behavior items

| item | domain | question description | response format | note |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| `cc_behavior_meat` | Behavior | “To what extent, if any, do you avoid high-emissions food products such as meat and dairy in order to help address climate change?” | 1 = not at all to 5 = a lot | Downstream mitigation-behavior item |
| `cc_behavior_travel` | Behavior | “To what extent, if any, do you seek lower-emissions travel alternatives in order to help address climate change?” | 1 = not at all to 5 = a lot | Downstream mitigation-behavior item |
| `cc_behavior_activ` | Behavior | “To what extent, if any, do you engage in political campaigning or activism to address climate change?” | 1 = not at all to 5 = a lot | Downstream public-engagement behavior |
| `cc_behavior_discuss` | Behavior | “To what extent, if any, do you discuss climate change with others?” | 1 = not at all to 5 = a lot | Downstream communication behavior |
| `cc_behavior_evacuate` | Behavior | “To what extent have you recently done or are currently doing the following to prepare for the impacts of climate change: create or maintain an emergency kit or evacuation plan?” | 1 = not at all to 5 = a lot | Downstream protective / adaptation behavior |
| `cc_behavior_move` | Behavior | “To what extent have you recently done or are currently doing the following to prepare for the impacts of climate change: consider moving to a different neighborhood or area?” | 1 = not at all to 5 = a lot | Downstream protective / adaptation behavior |

# 3. Exploratory data analysis

The EDA serves one primary goal: identify which repeated attitudinal variables form coherent, distinct, and intervention-relevant **belief-network nodes**. Four diagnostic tools are used in sequence — correlation structure, item screening, hierarchical clustering, and EFA — and composite decisions are made only after consulting all four.

## 3.1 Person-level averaged items

```{r participant-averages}
att_items_h <- screen_items_raw

df_att_person <- df_long_h |>
  dplyr::group_by(participant_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(across(any_of(att_items_h), mean_or_na),
                   .groups = "drop")

cat("Person-level averaged item dataset:",
    nrow(df_att_person), "x", ncol(df_att_person), "\n")
```

## 3.2 Descriptives

```{r attitude-descriptives}
psych::describe(df_att_person |> dplyr::select(-participant_id)) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("item") |>
  dplyr::select(item, n, mean, sd, median, min, max, skew, kurtosis) |>
  dplyr::mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 2)))
```

```{r attitude-distributions, fig.height=10}
df_att_person |>
  dplyr::select(-participant_id) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(),
                      names_to = "item", values_to = "value") |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~item, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  labs(title = "Person-level averaged attitude items (0–1 scale)",
       subtitle = "Averaged across all available waves after harmonisation",
       x = NULL, y = "Count")
```

The person-level averaged attitude items show a dataset that is fully usable for screening: all candidate variables have observations for all participants after recoding and averaging across available waves. At this stage, the main issue is therefore not participant-level missingness, but the shape, overlap, and interpretability of the resulting averaged variables.

The descriptives suggest that the sample leans clearly in a pro-climate direction on many of the core attitudinal items. This is especially evident for `cc1`, `cc5_world`, `cc_pol_car`, `cvcc9_cc`, `cvcc6`, and `cvcc4_should`, all of which have relatively high means and negative skew. In substantive terms, respondents tend on average to endorse the reality of climate change, report moderate to high concern, perceive substantial current and future harm, and support scientifically guided response and some climate policies. Several variables also show upper-end concentration, especially `cc1`, indicating that belief in climate change is already close to ceiling for a large share of respondents.

The harm items show a coherent descriptive pattern. Perceived harm is highest for the world in general and for poor communities, lower for local community and wealthy U.S. communities, and consistently higher for future harm than for present harm. This pattern is substantively sensible and suggests that respondents see climate change as both unequally distributed and worsening over time.

The norm-related variables are also differentiated in an interpretable way. `cvcc4_should` has the highest mean among the three norm-adjacent items, followed by `cvcc4_personal`, with `cvcc4_will` lowest. This suggests that respondents are more willing to endorse what people **should** do than to say they personally will do it, and are least willing to expect that others actually will do it. That already indicates that the injunctive, personal-intention, and descriptive-norm items should not be treated as interchangeable.

More peripheral variables such as `pol_ideology`, `cvcc_worryothers`, `ew5`, and `ew6` are closer to the midpoint and show less pronounced skew. The screening-only risk items `cc10`–`cc12` also have more centered distributions and less obvious ceiling structure than the main climate-attitude items, suggesting that they may behave differently from the dense pro-climate core.

The distribution plots reinforce these conclusions. Many variables remain visibly discrete and bounded even after averaging across waves, which is expected given the ordinal response formats and limited number of repeated measurements. Several items show clear ceiling tendency, while others such as `pol7`, `pol7_pi`, and the risk-perception items remain much coarser or more centered. These distributional features matter for later interpretation because they suggest that some variables reflect a broad pro-climate consensus in this sample, whereas others may capture more distinct or weakly aligned content.

## 3.3 Correlation structure

```{r attitude-corr}
df_att_mv <- df_att_person |>
  dplyr::select(-participant_id) |>
  dplyr::select(where(~ mean(!is.na(.x)) >= 0.90))

cor_att <- cor(df_att_mv, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

cat("Items entering multivariate screening:", ncol(df_att_mv), "\n")
cat(paste(colnames(df_att_mv), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

```{r attitude-corr-heatmap, fig.height=10, fig.width=10}
pheatmap(cor_att,
         clustering_method = "ward.D2",
         cutree_rows = 5, cutree_cols = 5,
         color = colorRampPalette(c("#2166ac","white","#d73027"))(100),
         display_numbers = TRUE, number_format = "%.2f",
         number_color = "black", fontsize_number = 6,
         fontsize_row = 9, fontsize_col = 9, angle_col = 45,
         main = "Item correlations — person-level averages",
         border_color = NA)
```

The correlation heatmap shows that the repeated attitude battery is dominated by one broad positive climate-attitude field. Most of the belief, concern, present-harm, future-harm, policy-support, response-orientation, and some norm-related items are strongly and positively associated with one another. This indicates that, at the between-person level, respondents who score high on one pro-climate dimension also tend to score high on many others.

The harm items are especially tightly integrated into this broader block. The `cc4_*` and `cc5_*` variables do not separate into sharply distinct present- and future-harm clusters. Instead, they are highly correlated both within and across the two families, suggesting that current and future harm perceptions are empirically very close in this sample. This does not rule out retaining separate present- and future-harm composites later, but it does mean that their distinction is likely to be more theoretical than strongly empirical.

`cc6` and `cvcc6` are also embedded deeply within the same dense correlation block. This suggests that general climate worry and endorsement of individual action are not behaving like isolated constructs; instead, they track the broader pro-climate field quite closely. Similarly, `cc1` and the analytically recoded `cc2` show substantial positive associations with the main attitudinal core, indicating that climate-change belief and attribution are aligned with concern, harm perception, and policy support.

By contrast, several variables appear more peripheral. `cvcc4_will`, `pol_ideology`, `pol7_pi`, `cvcc_worryothers`, `ew5`, and the risk-perception items do not sit as centrally inside the dense attitudinal block. They still relate to the broader system, but much more weakly. This is useful, because it suggests that these variables may add distinct information rather than simply duplicating the strongest pro-climate items.

Two variables stand out as especially weakly connected: `ew6` and `cc11`. Both show relatively low correlations with most other candidates. At this stage they appear to be among the least embedded variables in the candidate set and are therefore natural candidates for closer scrutiny in the later screening steps.

```{r attitude-redundancy, fig.height=4}
cor_long <- cor_att |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("item1") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-item1, names_to = "item2", values_to = "r") |>
  dplyr::filter(item1 < item2, !is.na(r), abs(r) > 0.80) |>
  dplyr::arrange(desc(abs(r)))

if (nrow(cor_long) > 0) {
  ggplot(cor_long,
         aes(x = r, y = reorder(paste(item1, "↔", item2), r))) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = 0.80, yend = paste(item1, "↔", item2)),
                 colour = "gray70") +
    geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#d73027") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", colour = "gray50") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    labs(title = "Highly correlated pairs (|r| > 0.80)",
         x = "Pearson r", y = NULL)
}
```

The redundancy plot sharpens the picture from the full heatmap by focusing on item pairs with correlations above `.80`. The clearest result is that redundancy is concentrated in the harm system. Many of the strongest pairwise associations involve combinations of `cc4_*` and `cc5_*` items, indicating that these variables are not only coherent but in several cases close to interchangeable at the between-person level.

Importantly, the strongest pairs are not limited to within-family comparisons such as present harm with present harm or future harm with future harm. Several very high correlations also occur across present- and future-harm items. This again suggests that the empirical distinction between present and future harm is modest relative to their large shared variance. If the final measurement model retains both, that choice should be understood as a substantively motivated simplification rather than a reflection of sharply separable empirical domains.

The redundancy plot also shows that `cc6` and `cvcc6` overlap strongly with the harm items. General worry and endorsement of individual action appear to track the same broad pro-climate dimension that is already captured by the harm perceptions. This does not make these items useless, but it does mean that they may contribute limited unique information once broader composites are formed.

Equally important is what does **not** appear in the high-correlation list. Variables such as `cvcc4_will`, `pol_ideology`, `pol7_pi`, `cvcc_worryothers`, `ew5`, `ew6`, and most of the risk-perception items do not show the same degree of redundancy with the dominant climate-attitude core. That suggests that some of these more peripheral variables may survive later screening precisely because they are less duplicative, even if they are not among the strongest correlates of the main pro-climate block.

::: callout-note
At this stage, the descriptives, distributions, correlation heatmap, and redundancy plot all suggest a dense and highly overlapping climate-attitude field, with especially strong redundancy among the harm items and substantial overlap between concern, harm, policy support, and climate-action orientation. The next EDA steps therefore ask a more refined question: which of these candidate variables remain well embedded yet sufficiently distinct to justify inclusion in a compact final node set once communality, partial-correlation structure, clustering, and factor solutions are taken into account?
:::

## 3.4 Item screening

```{r item-screening, fig.height=6}
df_screen <- df_att_mv |>
  dplyr::select(where(~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE) > 0)) |>
  dplyr::filter(complete.cases(dplyr::pick(everything())))

cat("Complete cases for screening EFA:", nrow(df_screen), "\n")

efa_screen <- psych::fa(df_screen, nfactors = 6,
                         rotate = "oblimin", fm = "ml")

pcor_mat <- corpcor::cor2pcor(cor(df_screen, use = "complete.obs"))
rownames(pcor_mat) <- colnames(pcor_mat) <- colnames(df_screen)
max_pcor <- apply(abs(pcor_mat), 1,
                  function(x) max(x[x < 1], na.rm = TRUE))

screening <- tibble::tibble(
  item     = rownames(efa_screen$loadings),
  h2       = round(as.numeric(efa_screen$communality), 3),
  max_pcor = round(max_pcor[rownames(efa_screen$loadings)], 3)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(status = dplyr::case_when(
    h2 < 0.20 & max_pcor < 0.25 ~ "Drop — isolated",
    h2 < 0.30                   ~ "Caution",
    TRUE                        ~ "Keep"))

screening |> dplyr::arrange(h2) |> print(n = 25)
```

```{r item-screening-plot, fig.height=6}
ggplot(screening,
       aes(x = h2, y = max_pcor, colour = status, label = item)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 3.5, max.overlaps = 25) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.20, linetype = "dashed", colour = "gray50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.25, linetype = "dashed", colour = "gray50") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Drop — isolated" = "#d73027",
                                  "Caution" = "#fc8d59",
                                  "Keep" = "#4393c3")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "Item screening — communality vs max partial correlation",
       subtitle = "h² < 0.20 and max pcor < 0.25 → isolated",
       x = "Communality (h²)", y = "Max partial correlation",
       colour = NULL)
```

The screening step shows that most candidate variables are at least moderately embedded in the averaged attitude system, but they are not equally strong. Only one item, `pol7_pi`, falls below both screening thresholds and is therefore clearly isolated in this dataset. Its communality is very low (`h² = 0.162`) and its maximum partial correlation is also weak (`max_pcor = 0.20`), making it the only straightforward drop at this stage.

Several other variables fall into a caution zone rather than a clear keep-or-drop category. Most notably, `cc11` has extremely low communality (`h² = 0.021`), while `cc10` and `cc12` also show weak shared variance relative to the rest of the battery. These three items therefore do not behave like strong members of the main climate-attitude field. However, because their maximum partial correlations are not negligible, they are better treated as weakly integrated or structurally distinct candidates than as outright noise.

By contrast, the core climate-attitude items all show high communalities and generally moderate-to-strong maximum partial correlations. This is especially true for the harm items, the policy items, `cc1`, `cc6`, `cvcc9_cc`, `cvcc6`, and `cvcc4_should`, all of which appear deeply embedded in the common attitudinal structure. The screening results therefore reinforce the earlier correlation plots: the main issue is not whether the core items belong to the system, but whether some of them are too redundant to all survive into a compact final node set.

## 3.5 Hierarchical clustering

```{r clustering-setup}
drop_items_screen <- screening |>
  dplyr::filter(status == "Drop — isolated") |>
  dplyr::pull(item)

kept_items <- setdiff(colnames(df_att_mv), drop_items_screen)
cat("Dropped by screening:", paste(drop_items_screen, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Retained:", paste(kept_items, collapse = ", "), "\n")

df_kept <- df_att_mv |>
  dplyr::select(all_of(kept_items)) |>
  dplyr::filter(complete.cases(dplyr::pick(everything())))

cat("Complete cases:", nrow(df_kept), "\n")

cor_kept <- cor(df_kept, use = "complete.obs")
dist_cor <- as.dist(1 - cor_kept)
```

```{r clustering-all, fig.height=10, fig.width=12}
hc_ward     <- hclust(dist_cor, method = "ward.D2")
hc_average  <- hclust(dist_cor, method = "average")
hc_complete <- hclust(dist_cor, method = "complete")

mi_matrix <- matrix(NA, ncol = ncol(df_kept), nrow = ncol(df_kept))
colnames(mi_matrix) <- rownames(mi_matrix) <- colnames(df_kept)

for (i in seq_len(ncol(df_kept))) {
  for (j in i:ncol(df_kept)) {
    mi_matrix[i, j] <- infotheo::mutinformation(
      infotheo::discretize(df_kept[[i]]),
      infotheo::discretize(df_kept[[j]])
    )
    mi_matrix[j, i] <- mi_matrix[i, j]
  }
}

hc_mi <- hclust(
  as.dist(1 - mi_matrix / max(mi_matrix, na.rm = TRUE)),
  method = "ward.D2"
)

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1))

plot(hc_ward, main = "Ward.D2", cex = 0.75, xlab = "", sub = "")
rect.hclust(hc_ward, k = 8, border = 2:6)

plot(hc_average, main = "Average", cex = 0.75, xlab = "", sub = "")
rect.hclust(hc_average, k = 8, border = 2:6)

plot(hc_complete, main = "Complete", cex = 0.75, xlab = "", sub = "")
rect.hclust(hc_complete, k = 8, border = 2:6)

plot(hc_mi, main = "Mutual information — Ward.D2", cex = 0.75, xlab = "", sub = "")
rect.hclust(hc_mi, k = 8, border = 2:6)

par(op)
```

The clustering results add useful structure to the dense correlation picture. Across linkage methods, and especially in the mutual-information dendrogram, the candidate items organize into a small number of recurring groups rather than a large set of sharply independent domains.

The most stable and interpretable cluster is the future-harm family: `cc5_world`, `cc5_wealthUS`, `cc5_poorUS`, and `cc5_comm` group tightly together. A second nearby cluster contains the present-harm items together with the more general belief/concern indicators `cc3` and `cc6`, suggesting that present harm is psychologically closer to immediate climate concern than to a wholly separate harm domain.

A third cluster contains `cc1`, `cc2`, `pol7`, the two policy-support items, `cvcc9_cc`, and `cvcc6`, with `pol_ideology` adjacent to that set. This is best read as a broader belief–policy–response orientation cluster rather than as a set of clearly separate constructs. The norm triplet — `cvcc4_should`, `cvcc4_will`, and `cvcc4_personal` — forms a clean local cluster of its own, which supports the idea that these three items belong to the same general norm/intention family even though they should not automatically be treated as the same construct.

Finally, `ew5` and `ew6` sit in a peripheral cluster together with `cc10`–`cc12` and `cvcc_worryothers`. This is important: it suggests that weather risk, psychometric risk perception, and perceived public worry are related side-content, but they are not tightly fused with the dominant belief–harm–policy field. That makes them plausible screening candidates, but weaker candidates for the final compact node set.

## 3.6 PCA

```{r pca-scree, fig.height=5}
eig <- eigen(cor_kept)

data.frame(component = seq_along(eig$values),
           eigenvalue = eig$values) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = component, y = eigenvalue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(eigenvalue, 2)),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "Scree plot — averaged attitude items",
       x = "Component", y = "Eigenvalue")
```

```{r pca-loadings, fig.height=8}
n_pc <- min(5, ncol(cor_kept))
loadings_pca <- as.data.frame(
  eig$vectors[, 1:n_pc] %*% diag(sqrt(eig$values[1:n_pc])))
rownames(loadings_pca) <- colnames(cor_kept)
colnames(loadings_pca) <- paste0("PC", seq_len(n_pc))

pheatmap(loadings_pca, cluster_cols = FALSE,
         clustering_method = "ward.D2",
         color = colorRampPalette(c("#d73027","white","#2166ac"))(100),
         display_numbers = TRUE, number_format = "%.2f",
         number_color = "black", fontsize_number = 8, fontsize_row = 9,
         main = "PCA loadings — averaged attitude items",
         border_color = NA)
```

The PCA results show a very strong first component. The scree plot is dominated by PC1 (`eigenvalue = 14.95`), with a steep drop to PC2 (`1.73`) and then a long shallow tail. This is the clearest indication in the full EDA that the repeated attitude battery is organized primarily as one broad between-person climate-attitude dimension rather than as many equally strong latent domains.

The loading heatmap reinforces that interpretation. Most of the core climate items — belief, concern, harm, policy support, response orientation, and some norm-related content — load heavily on PC1, while later components capture more local contrasts at the margin. In particular, the later components pick up side structure involving weather risk, public worry, and the psychometric risk items, but these are clearly secondary to the dominant first component.

This does not mean that only one composite should be retained. Rather, it means that any final node set must be understood as a parsimonious summary carved out of a very dense and largely shared pro-climate field. The purpose of later composite construction is therefore not to recover many empirically independent subdomains, but to retain a small number of substantively interpretable nodes from a strongly overlapping system.

## 3.7 EFA

```{r efa-parallel, fig.height=5}
psych::fa.parallel(df_kept, fa = "fa", fm = "ml",
                   main = "Parallel analysis — averaged attitude items")
```

```{r efa-solutions}
safe_round <- function(x, d = 3) {
  v <- tryCatch(as.numeric(x), error = function(e) NA_real_)
  if (!length(v) || all(is.na(v))) return(NA)
  round(v[1], d)
}

for (nf in 4:7) {
  cat("\n\n=== EFA:", nf, "factors ===\n")
  fit <- psych::fa(df_kept, nfactors = nf, rotate = "oblimin", fm = "ml")
  print(fit$loadings, cutoff = 0.30, sort = TRUE)
  cat("RMSEA:", safe_round(fit$RMSEA["RMSEA"]),
      "  TLI:", safe_round(fit$TLI),
      "  Var:", round(sum(fit$values[1:nf]) /
                       length(fit$values) * 100, 1), "%\n")
}
```

```{r efa-best, fig.height=9}
efa_best     <- psych::fa(df_kept, nfactors = 6,
                           rotate = "oblimin", fm = "ml")
loadings_mat <- as.data.frame(unclass(efa_best$loadings))

pheatmap(loadings_mat, cluster_cols = FALSE,
         clustering_method = "ward.D2",
         color = colorRampPalette(c("#d73027","white","#2166ac"))(100),
         display_numbers = TRUE, number_format = "%.2f",
         number_color = "black", fontsize_number = 7, fontsize_row = 9,
         main = "EFA loadings — 6-factor solution", border_color = NA)
```

The EFA results suggest that the data support more than one factor, but not in a way that argues for a very large final node set. Parallel analysis points upward, but the practical interpretation of the factor solutions is more important than the raw recommended count alone. The 4-factor solution is still fairly coarse (`RMSEA = 0.088`, `TLI = 0.900`), the 5-factor solution improves somewhat (`RMSEA = 0.080`, `TLI = 0.918`), and the 6- and 7-factor solutions improve fit further (`RMSEA = 0.074` and `0.064`; `TLI = 0.930` and `0.947`, respectively). However, the gain from 6 to 7 factors is modest, and the 7-factor solution mainly adds complexity rather than a clearly indispensable new construct.

The 6-factor solution is the most interpretable compromise. One factor is centered on policy support, response orientation, climate-action endorsement, and political positioning (`cc_pol_tax`, `cc_pol_car`, `cvcc9_cc`, `cvcc6`, `pol7`, and to a lesser extent `pol_ideology`). A second factor is a very clean norm/intention factor made up of `cvcc4_should`, `cvcc4_will`, and `cvcc4_personal`. A third factor captures a future/localized harm cluster, especially `cc5_wealthUS`, `cc5_comm`, and `cc5_poorUS`. A fourth factor is a weather-risk/preparedness factor anchored by `ew5` and `ew6`. A fifth factor is a general belief / problem-recognition factor centered on `cc1`, `cc2`, `cc3`, and `cc4_world`. The remaining harm items show cross-loadings rather than forming fully separate domains, which is consistent with the redundancy seen earlier.

Equally important is what does *not* load cleanly. `cc10`, `cc11`, and `cc12` do not emerge as a strong, coherent retained factor in any practically compelling way. They look more like a weak psychometric side block than like central candidates for the final belief network. `cvcc_worryothers` also remains comparatively diffuse, and `pol7_pi` has already dropped out at the earlier screening stage. Overall, the EFA supports keeping a compact core of belief/concern, harm, policy/response, norms, politics, and weather risk, while treating the remaining candidates as auxiliary or screening-only variables rather than as final nodes.

## 3.8 Wave-5 behavioral EDA

```{r behavior-descriptives}
psych::describe(df_w5_h |> dplyr::select(any_of(beh_items))) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("item") |>
  dplyr::select(item, n, mean, sd, median, min, max, skew, kurtosis) |>
  dplyr::mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 2)))
```

```{r behavior-distributions, fig.height=4}
df_w5_h |>
  dplyr::select(any_of(beh_items)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(),
                      names_to = "item", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "#E07B7B", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~item, scales = "free_y", ncol = 6) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  labs(title = "Wave-5 behavioral items (N = 870)",
       x = NULL, y = "Count")
```

```{r behavior-corr, fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
cor_beh <- df_w5_h |>
  dplyr::select(any_of(beh_items)) |>
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

pheatmap(cor_beh, clustering_method = "ward.D2",
         color = colorRampPalette(c("white", "#F1948A"))(100),
         display_numbers = TRUE, number_format = "%.2f",
         number_color = "black", fontsize_number = 9,
         fontsize_row = 9, fontsize_col = 9,
         main = "Behavioral item correlations (wave 5)",
         border_color = NA)
```

```{r behavior-efa}
df_beh <- df_w5_h |>
  dplyr::select(any_of(beh_items)) |>
  dplyr::filter(complete.cases(dplyr::pick(everything())))

psych::fa.parallel(df_beh, fa = "fa", fm = "ml",
                   main = "Parallel analysis — behavioral items")
```

```{r behavior-efa-solutions}
for (nf in 1:3) {
  cat("\n=== Behavioral EFA:", nf, "factor(s) ===\n")
  fit <- psych::fa(df_beh, nfactors = nf,
                   rotate = if (nf == 1) "none" else "oblimin",
                   fm = "ml")
  print(fit$loadings, cutoff = 0.30, sort = TRUE)
  cat("RMSEA:", safe_round(fit$RMSEA[["RMSEA"]]),
      " TLI:", safe_round(fit$TLI), "\n")
}
```

The behavioral items show a much less favorable distribution than the attitude items: all six behaviors have relatively low means and strong positive skew, indicating that these actions are less common and more unevenly distributed than pro-climate attitudes in the sample. In particular, `cc_behavior_activ` and `cc_behavior_move` are concentrated near zero, which suggests that political activism and relocation are relatively uncommon behaviors.

The factor results show some multidimensionality, but the evidence is mixed. The one-factor solution is acceptable but not especially strong (`RMSEA = 0.102`, `TLI = 0.936`), whereas the two-factor solution fits clearly better (`RMSEA = 0.058`, `TLI = 0.980`). However, that second factor is relatively thin: it is driven primarily by `cc_behavior_move`, with only partial support from `cc_behavior_evacuate`. The three-factor solution is not trustworthy, with degenerate loadings and inadmissible fit output.

Substantively, the two-factor pattern is interpretable as a contrast between more routine, active mitigation behaviors (`meat`, `travel`, `activism`, `discussion`) and more protective or high-cost adaptation behaviors (`evacuate`, `move`). At the same time, the protective side is much less robust psychometrically than the active side. This means that the behavior block is best treated as clearly downstream but measurement-wise somewhat thinner than the main attitude block. For later modeling, a broad downstream `climate_behavior` composite is defensible as the primary outcome, while an active-versus-protective split can be retained as a secondary sensitivity analysis if needed.

## 3.9 Composite decisions

**Composite decisions — integrating the full EDA**

The EDA indicates that the candidate battery is organized primarily as a dense shared pro-climate attitude field rather than as many sharply independent domains. The purpose of the final composites is therefore not to retain every variable that showed empirical signal, but to construct a compact, interpretable node set that avoids unnecessary duplication while still representing the main substantive domains.

### `belief_concern` — `cc1` + `cc6`

`cc1` and `cc6` are retained together as the final belief/concern composite. `cc1` captures endorsement that climate change is happening, while `cc6` captures personal worry or concern. Both are strongly embedded in the broader attitudinal field, and both load on the general belief / problem-recognition factor in the later EFA, although `cc6` does so more weakly than `cc1`. At the same time, the clustering results show that `cc1` and `cc6` are not closest neighbors: `cc6` sits nearer the present-harm / concern cluster, whereas `cc1` sits nearer the broader belief / policy / attribution cluster. The composite is therefore best understood as a theory-guided combination of two complementary climate-belief facets rather than as a pair singled out by local clustering alone.

`cc3` is not retained because it plays a very similar substantive role to `cc6` but has narrower temporal coverage. `cc2` is also not retained as a final node: although it behaves reasonably well in screening and aligns with the broader belief field, it depends on an analytic recoding and does not add a sufficiently clean final domain beyond `cc1` and `cc6`.

### `harm_present` — `cc4_world`, `cc4_wealthUS`, `cc4_poorUS`, `cc4_comm`

The four present-harm items are retained as one composite, but this decision is somewhat more theory-guided than the earlier wording suggested. The items are strongly intercorrelated and clearly belong to the broader harm system, which favors retaining them together. However, the 6-factor EFA does not place them all on one clean present-harm factor: `cc4_world` loads with the general belief / problem-recognition factor, `cc4_wealthUS` and `cc4_comm` load on a different harm-related factor, and `cc4_poorUS` sits between these patterns. The retained composite is therefore justified mainly because the four items ask parallel present-harm questions across different targets and remain highly redundant empirically, not because they form a perfectly unified EFA cluster.

### `harm_future` — `cc5_world`, `cc5_wealthUS`, `cc5_poorUS`, `cc5_comm`

The four future-harm items are retained as one composite. Compared with the present-harm family, the future-harm items are somewhat cleaner empirically: they cluster more tightly, show very strong internal coherence, and remain one of the clearest high-redundancy families in the battery. Even here, however, the EDA shows substantial cross-family overlap with present harm. Retaining `harm_future` separately is therefore defensible because the present/future distinction is substantively meaningful and built into the survey design, not because the two families are sharply distinct empirical domains.

### `policy_support` — `cc_pol_tax` + `cc_pol_car`

The two direct policy items are retained as the final policy-support composite. They are parallel in wording and response format, correlate strongly, and load consistently within the broader policy / response field. `pol7` is not retained as part of this composite because it is a binary economic-tradeoff item rather than a direct policy-support indicator. Although it aligns with the same broader field, it is coarser and conceptually more mixed than the two policy items.

### `trust_science` — `cvcc9_cc`

`cvcc9_cc` is retained as a single-item node. It loads with the broader policy / response field, but its wording is conceptually specific: it captures deference to expert-guided climate response rather than direct policy support or personal climate action. Keeping it as a single-item node is therefore more defensible than folding it into the policy composite.

### `social_norms` — `cvcc4_should`

`cvcc4_should` is retained as the final norm-related node. The EDA shows that `cvcc4_should`, `cvcc4_will`, and `cvcc4_personal` form a coherent local norm/intention family, but they reflect different constructs. `cvcc4_should` captures an **injunctive norm**: what people ought to do. It is retained because this is the clearest norm construct among the available candidates and is the most defensible standalone indicator of perceived normative obligation around lower-carbon behavior. `cvcc4_will` is excluded because it reflects a **descriptive expectation** about whether others will act, and `cvcc4_personal` is excluded because it reflects personal intention rather than a social norm. The COVID framing remains a limitation, but among the available candidates `cvcc4_should` provides the clearest measure of perceived injunctive norms.

### `politics` — `pol_ideology`

`pol_ideology` is retained as the political background/context node. It is clearly related to the broader climate-attitude field but remains more peripheral than the core climate items, so it is best treated as contextual positioning rather than part of the attitudinal core itself. `pol7` and especially `pol7_pi` are not retained as final nodes: `pol7` overlaps with the broader policy / politics dimension but is too coarse and mixed for the final compact node set, while `pol7_pi` is the only item that clearly fails screening as isolated.

### `weather_risk_prep` — `ew5` (ALT-SPEC: `ew6` excluded)

**Note (2026-09-04): this section describes the EDA-stage screening result, not the final composite used in this file.** `ew5` and `ew6` emerged from screening as a coherent weather-risk/preparedness pair (see EDA above), but this file implements the ALT-SPEC sensitivity definition (see note at top of file): `weather_risk_prep` is `ew5` alone. `ew6` (self-reported preparedness *behavior*) is excluded from the final composite because it measures a different construct than worry/risk perception and was empirically more weakly connected to the rest of the system. It remains listed in the candidate/screening variables above and in the codebook because it was a genuine candidate at that stage — it is simply not part of the final node used in the SCM and all downstream models in this file.

### Downstream behavior block — `climate_behavior`

The wave-5 behavior items are retained only as downstream outcomes and not as part of the core belief network. The behavioral EDA suggests some multidimensionality, with a plausible split between more routine mitigation behaviors and thinner protective/adaptation behaviors. However, that split is not robust enough to serve as the primary measurement choice. For the main extended analysis, the most defensible outcome is therefore a single broad `climate_behavior` composite, with more differentiated behavior splits treated only as supplementary sensitivity analyses.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
### Variables not retained as final nodes

- `cc2`: empirically viable in screening, but depends on an analytic recoding and overlaps heavily with the broader belief field
- `cc3`: substantively similar to `cc6`, but with narrower temporal coverage
- `cvcc6`: strongly embedded but conceptually redundant with the broader policy / response / concern field
- `cvcc4_will`: descriptive expectation about others’ likely behavior, not the retained injunctive norm item
- `cvcc4_personal`: personal intention, not a social expectation about others
- `cvcc_worryothers`: related but comparatively diffuse and peripheral, without a compelling case for a standalone final node
- `pol7`: useful in screening, but too coarse and conceptually mixed for the final compact node set
- `pol7_pi`: the only item that clearly fails screening as isolated
- `cc10`, `cc11`, `cc12`: weak and diffuse psychometric risk-perception side block, not central enough for the final network

**Bottom line.** The final measurement model should remain compact. The most defensible retained nodes are `belief_concern`, `harm_present`, `harm_future`, `policy_support`, `trust_science`, `social_norms`, `politics`, and `weather_risk_prep`, with `climate_behavior` treated separately as a downstream outcome block. This preserves the main substantive domains while avoiding unnecessary duplication from the broader, highly overlapping attitudinal field.
:::

**Composite-decision summary.** Taken together, the EDA indicates that the candidate battery is organized primarily as a dense shared pro-climate attitude field rather than as many sharply independent domains. The final node set should therefore be understood as a compact, theory-guided summary carved out of that broader overlapping system, not as a set of empirically independent latent blocks. On that basis, we retain `belief_concern`, `harm_present`, `harm_future`, `policy_support`, `trust_science`, `social_norms`, `politics`, and `weather_risk_prep` as the main attitude/context nodes, and treat `climate_behavior` separately as a downstream wave-5 outcome. This preserves the main substantive domains while avoiding unnecessary duplication from the broader attitudinal field. The present-versus-future harm distinction is retained mainly for substantive interpretability rather than because the two families are sharply separable empirically, whereas `trust_science`, `social_norms`, and `politics` are retained as substantively specific single-item nodes.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 4. Composite construction

This section converts the retained item set into the compact node set used in the later network and causal-discovery analyses. All repeated-attitude composites are constructed from the **person-level averaged items** created in Section 3.1. The resulting nodes therefore represent stable between-person positions rather than wave-specific states.

## 4.1 Main attitude composites

```{r composite-construction}
df_main <- df_att_person |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    participant_id,

    belief_concern = rowMeans(
      dplyr::pick(cc1, cc6),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    harm_present = rowMeans(
      dplyr::pick(cc4_world, cc4_wealthUS, cc4_poorUS, cc4_comm),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    harm_future = rowMeans(
      dplyr::pick(cc5_world, cc5_wealthUS, cc5_poorUS, cc5_comm),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    policy_support = rowMeans(
      dplyr::pick(cc_pol_tax, cc_pol_car),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    trust_science = cvcc9_cc,

    social_norms = cvcc4_should,

    politics = pol_ideology,

    # ALT-SPEC (sensitivity check, see note at top of file): weather_risk_prep
    # redefined as ew5 alone. ew6 (preparedness behavior) is excluded here --
    # it measures a different construct (self-reported protective behavior,
    # not worry/risk perception) and was empirically far more weakly
    # connected to the rest of the system (see composite-validation numbers
    # in the original file). Variable name is left unchanged so nothing
    # downstream needs to be touched.
    weather_risk_prep = ew5
  )

cat("Main composite dataset:", nrow(df_main), "x", ncol(df_main), "\n")
cat("Any missing values in df_main:", any(is.na(df_main)), "\n")

colSums(is.na(df_main))
```

::: callout-note
The main belief-network dataset is intentionally compact. It retains the final node set supported by the EDA: `belief_concern`, `harm_present`, `harm_future`, `policy_support`, `trust_science`, `social_norms`, `politics`, and `weather_risk_prep`.

The screening-only variables from Section 3 are **not** carried forward into `df_main`. Their role was to test whether they added distinct or necessary structure; the final network is built only from the retained composite set.
:::

## 4.2 Sensitivity analysis for `cc1` coding

```{r cc1-sensitivity}
df_long_cc1 <- df_long |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cc1_mid = recode_cc1_midpoint(cc1),
    cc1_na  = recode_cc1_dropdk(cc1),
    cc6_h   = rescale01(na_special(cc6), from = c(1, 4))
  )

df_cc1_sens <- df_long_cc1 |>
  dplyr::group_by(participant_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    bel_mid = mean_or_na(rowMeans(cbind(cc1_mid, cc6_h), na.rm = TRUE)),
    bel_na  = mean_or_na(rowMeans(cbind(cc1_na,  cc6_h), na.rm = FALSE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cat(
  "Correlation between midpoint and drop-DK versions:",
  round(cor(df_cc1_sens$bel_mid, df_cc1_sens$bel_na, use = "complete.obs"), 3),
  "\n"
)
cat("Missing in drop-DK version:", sum(is.na(df_cc1_sens$bel_na)), "\n")
```

::: callout-note
This sensitivity check asks whether the final `belief_concern` composite depends materially on how the “don’t know” response in `cc1` is handled. If the midpoint-coded and drop-DK versions correlate almost perfectly, the midpoint version can be retained as a pragmatic choice that preserves sample size without changing the substantive result.
:::

## 4.3 Wave-5 downstream behavior composite

```{r climate-behavior-composite}
df_behavior_w5 <- df_w5_h |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    participant_id,
    beh_meat     = cc_behavior_meat,
    beh_travel   = cc_behavior_travel,
    beh_activ    = cc_behavior_activ,
    beh_discuss  = cc_behavior_discuss,
    beh_evacuate = cc_behavior_evacuate,
    beh_move     = cc_behavior_move,

    climate_behavior = rowMeans(
      dplyr::pick(
        beh_meat, beh_travel, beh_activ,
        beh_discuss, beh_evacuate, beh_move
      ),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

cat("Wave-5 behavior dataset:", nrow(df_behavior_w5), "\n")
cat("Missing climate_behavior:", sum(is.na(df_behavior_w5$climate_behavior)), "\n")
cat(
  "climate_behavior alpha =",
  round(psych::alpha(
    df_behavior_w5 |>
      dplyr::select(
        beh_meat, beh_travel, beh_activ,
        beh_discuss, beh_evacuate, beh_move
      )
  )$total$raw_alpha, 3),
  "\n"
)
```

::: callout-note
The wave-5 behavior block is treated as a **downstream outcome** rather than as part of the core belief network. Although the EDA suggested some possible multidimensionality, the primary outcome used in the main extended analysis is a single broad `climate_behavior` composite. More differentiated behavioral splits can still be explored later as sensitivity analyses if needed, but they are not part of the primary measurement model.
:::

## 4.4 Analysis datasets

```{r analysis-datasets}
df_extended <- df_main |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    df_behavior_w5 |>
      dplyr::select(participant_id, climate_behavior),
    by = "participant_id"
  )

cat("Main belief-network dataset: N =", nrow(df_main), "\n")
cat("Extended (+ behavior) dataset: N =", nrow(df_extended), "\n")
```

::: callout-important
**Final data structure**

| Dataset | N | Source | Purpose |
|----------------|---------------:|----------------------|-------------------|
| `df_main` | `r nrow(df_main)` | Person-level averages of retained repeated-attitude items | Main belief-network and causal-discovery analyses |
| `df_extended` | `r nrow(df_extended)` | `df_main` plus wave-5 `climate_behavior` | Extended downstream behavior analysis |

The main analyses are based on stable participant-level averages of the retained attitude nodes. The extended dataset adds the downstream wave-5 behavioral outcome so that later sections can test whether the stable belief network is meaningfully related to later climate-related behavior.
:::

```{r}
df_long_h_pre5 <- df_long_h |> dplyr::filter(wave <= 4)

df_att_person_pre5 <- df_long_h_pre5 |>
  dplyr::group_by(participant_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(across(any_of(att_items_h), mean_or_na), .groups = "drop")

df_main_pre5 <- df_att_person_pre5 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    participant_id,
    belief_concern    = rowMeans(dplyr::pick(cc1, cc6), na.rm = TRUE),
    harm_present      = rowMeans(dplyr::pick(cc4_world, cc4_wealthUS, cc4_poorUS, cc4_comm), na.rm = TRUE),
    harm_future       = rowMeans(dplyr::pick(cc5_world, cc5_wealthUS, cc5_poorUS, cc5_comm), na.rm = TRUE),
    policy_support    = rowMeans(dplyr::pick(cc_pol_tax, cc_pol_car), na.rm = TRUE),
    trust_science     = cvcc9_cc,
    social_norms      = cvcc4_should,
    politics          = pol_ideology,
    weather_risk_prep = ew5  # ALT-SPEC: ew5 alone, see note at top of file
  )

df_main_allwave     <- df_main
df_extended_allwave <- df_extended

df_main     <- df_main_pre5
df_extended <- df_main_pre5 |>
  dplyr::inner_join(df_behavior_w5 |> dplyr::select(participant_id, climate_behavior), by = "participant_id")
```

# 5. Composite validation

This section checks whether the retained composites behave as intended after construction. The aim is not to re-run the item-level EDA, but to verify that the final node set is coherent, interpretable, and suitable for the later network analyses.

## 5.1 Internal consistency

```{r composite-reliability}
r2 <- function(x, y) round(cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs"), 3)

cat("=== Main attitude composites ===\n")

cat("belief_concern r(cc1, cc6) =",
    r2(df_att_person$cc1, df_att_person$cc6), "\n")

cat("harm_present alpha =",
    round(psych::alpha(
      df_att_person |>
        dplyr::select(cc4_world, cc4_wealthUS, cc4_poorUS, cc4_comm)
    )$total$raw_alpha, 3), "\n")

cat("harm_future alpha =",
    round(psych::alpha(
      df_att_person |>
        dplyr::select(cc5_world, cc5_wealthUS, cc5_poorUS, cc5_comm)
    )$total$raw_alpha, 3), "\n")

cat("policy_support r(cc_pol_tax, cc_pol_car) =",
    r2(df_att_person$cc_pol_tax, df_att_person$cc_pol_car), "\n")

cat("weather_risk_prep (ALT-SPEC) = ew5 alone -- no internal-consistency stat applicable\n")
cat("  [reference only] r(ew5, ew6) =",
    r2(df_att_person$ew5, df_att_person$ew6),
    "-- NOT used to construct weather_risk_prep in this file; ew6 is excluded\n")

cat("trust_science = single item (cvcc9_cc)\n")
cat("social_norms = single item (cvcc4_should)\n")
cat("politics = single item (pol_ideology)\n")

cat("\n=== Downstream behavior composite ===\n")
cat("climate_behavior alpha =",
    round(psych::alpha(
      df_behavior_w5 |>
        dplyr::select(
          beh_meat, beh_travel, beh_activ,
          beh_discuss, beh_evacuate, beh_move
        )
    )$total$raw_alpha, 3), "\n")
```

::: callout-note
The strongest multi-item composites are expected to be the harm nodes, because they are made from parallel item families. `belief_concern`, `policy_support`, and `weather_risk_prep` are intentionally compact and are therefore evaluated mainly through their inter-item correlations rather than long-form reliability alone. `trust_science`, `social_norms`, and `politics` are single-item nodes by design and should be interpreted as such.

For the downstream outcome, the main question is whether the six behavioral items are coherent enough to justify a broad summary index of climate-related behavior at wave 5. The composite does not need to be perfectly homogeneous to serve that role, but it should show at least moderate internal consistency.
:::

```{r climate-behavior-distribution, fig.height=4}
df_behavior_w5 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = climate_behavior)) +
```

::: callout-note
These plots show whether the retained composites preserve usable between-person variation after averaging and aggregation. Skew is not itself a problem here, but it does matter for later modeling because several of the retained nodes remain bounded and visibly non-normal. That is why the network analysis uses a nonparanormal transformation rather than the raw composite scores.
:::

## 5.3 Composite correlation matrix

```{r composite-corr, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
cor_composites <- df_main |>
  dplyr::select(-participant_id) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

pheatmap(
  cor_composites,
  clustering_method = "ward.D2",
```

::: callout-note
This matrix is the compact summary of the final belief-network node set. The key empirical question is whether the retained nodes still form one dense positive block, or whether some now behave more like peripheral contextual variables. Based on the item-level EDA, a dense positive climate-attitude field is expected, with especially strong overlap among `belief_concern`, the two harm composites, and `policy_support`, and somewhat more peripheral placement for `politics` and `weather_risk_prep`.
:::

## 5.4 Stable attitudes and downstream behavior

```{r behavior-att-cors, fig.height=5}
df_extended |>
  dplyr::select(-participant_id) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("from") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-from, names_to = "to", values_to = "r") |>
  dplyr::filter(to == "climate_behavior",
                from != "climate_behavior") |>
  dplyr::arrange(desc(r)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(from, r), y = r, fill = r > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#2166ac", "FALSE" = "#d73027"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
```
