```{r behavior-att-cors, fig.height=5}
    title = "Stable attitudes and later climate behavior",
    subtitle = "Bivariate associations in the extended sample",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Pearson r"
  )
```

::: callout-note
This figure is a descriptive bridge to the later extended analyses. It does not identify causal effects, but it shows which stable attitude domains are most strongly associated with later climate-related behavior. This is especially relevant for `social_norms`, `policy_support`, and `belief_concern`, because those are the nodes most likely to matter for intervention-oriented interpretation later on.
:::

## 5.5 Validation summary before network analysis

**Composite-validation summary.** The retained measurement model is compact but usable. The two harm composites are the most internally coherent nodes, `belief_concern` and `policy_support` are strong short composites, and `weather_risk_prep` is better understood as a weaker contextual index than as a central ideological dimension. At the same time, the retained composites remain strongly intercorrelated, so they should not be interpreted as sharply independent latent domains. Rather, they are a parsimonious summary of a dense and overlapping between-person climate-attitude field. The downstream `climate_behavior` composite is sufficiently coherent for use as a broad wave-5 behavioral outcome, but it remains conceptually broader and measurement-wise thinner than the main attitude block.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 6. Network analysis

This section estimates the **conditional association structure** among the retained composite nodes. The goal is descriptive: to identify which nodes remain uniquely connected once the shared variance of the broader climate-attitude field is partialled out.

The network estimated here is a **Gaussian graphical model (GGM)**. In a GGM, each edge represents a **partial correlation**: the association between two nodes after conditioning on all other nodes in the graph. Equivalently, the edge weights are derived from the inverse covariance matrix (the precision matrix). The resulting graph is **undirected** and should be interpreted as a map of unique between-person associations, not as a causal graph.

A GGM is appropriate here because the retained nodes are **person-level composite scores**, not raw categorical items. Most nodes are either averages of multiple ordinal items or averages across repeated waves, so they take on many distinct values and behave more like bounded continuous variables than like binary or nominal measurements. At the same time, these composites remain visibly skewed and bounded, so the analysis uses a **nonparanormal transformation** before estimation. This yields a semiparametric Gaussian-copula version of the GGM, which is more defensible than assuming strict multivariate normality of the raw composite scores.

The main network is estimated on the eight retained attitudinal/context nodes. The extended network adds `climate_behavior` as a downstream wave-5 outcome. Even in the extended graph, however, the estimated network remains an undirected conditional association map rather than a directional model.

## 6.1 Node sets and transformation

```{r network-setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(huge)
  library(qgraph)
  library(bootnet)
})

main_nodes <- c(
  "belief_concern",
  "harm_present",
  "harm_future",
  "policy_support",
  "trust_science",
  "social_norms",
  "politics",
  "weather_risk_prep"
)


extended_nodes <- c(main_nodes, "climate_behavior")

node_labels <- c(
  belief_concern       = "Belief /\nConcern",
  harm_present         = "Present\nHarm",
  harm_future          = "Future\nHarm",
  policy_support       = "Policy\nSupport",
  trust_science = "Trust\nScience",
  social_norms         = "Social\nNorms",
  politics             = "Politics",
  weather_risk_prep    = "Weather\nRisk",
  climate_behavior     = "Climate\nBehavior"
)

node_colors <- c(
  # 2026-09-05: lightened further ("more pastel-y, like GGM") -- must stay
  # byte-for-byte identical to node_family_colors in r_patches/03_figure_style.R
  belief_concern       = "#D5ECF9",
  harm_present         = "#D5ECF9",
  harm_future          = "#D5ECF9",
  policy_support       = "#D5ECF9",
  trust_science = "#D5ECF9",
  social_norms         = "#EDDEF2",
  politics             = "#D5F1E2",
  weather_risk_prep    = "#FCEBD1",
  climate_behavior     = "#F8D7D2"
)

# main network data
df_net_main_raw <- df_main |>
  dplyr::select(all_of(main_nodes))

df_net_main <- df_net_main_raw |>
  huge::huge.npn(npn.func = "truncation") |>
  as.data.frame()

colnames(df_net_main) <- main_nodes

# extended network data
df_net_ext_raw <- df_extended |>
  dplyr::select(all_of(extended_nodes))

df_net_ext <- df_net_ext_raw |>
  huge::huge.npn(npn.func = "truncation") |>
  as.data.frame()

colnames(df_net_ext) <- extended_nodes

cat("Main nodes:", paste(main_nodes, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Extended nodes:", paste(extended_nodes, collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

::: callout-note
A Gaussian-copula interpretation means that the observed variables do not themselves need to be normally distributed. Instead, it assumes that their dependence structure can be approximated by a multivariate normal distribution after monotone marginal transformation. The nonparanormal transformation is used here to make that assumption more plausible for bounded, skewed composite scores without claiming that the raw data are truly normal. In `huge::huge.npn(..., npn.func = "truncation")`, each node is transformed separately by ranking the observed values, converting those ranks to empirical cumulative probabilities, shrinking the most extreme probabilities slightly inward to avoid infinities, and then mapping them to inverse-normal scores. This preserves rank order but changes spacing, so skewed or ceiling-prone marginals become more compatible with Gaussian-based methods. The transformation therefore does not add causal information or literally normalize the data; it is a semiparametric preprocessing step that makes GGMs and Gaussian conditional-independence tests more defensible for these retained composite nodes.

Because the network is estimated on retained composite scores rather than on the original categorical item responses, a Gaussian graphical model is more appropriate here than an Ising model or a mixed graphical model. Those alternatives would be more natural if the analysis were conducted directly at the raw item level.
:::

## 6.2 Transformed distributions

```{r npn-distributions, fig.height=9}
# df_net_main |>
#   tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(),
#                       names_to = "node", values_to = "value") |>
#   ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
#   geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
#   facet_wrap(~node, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
#   theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
#   labs(
#     title = "Main network nodes after nonparanormal transformation",
#     subtitle = "Transformed participant-level composite scores",
#     x = NULL,
#     y = "Count"
#   )

df_net_ext |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(),
                      names_to = "node", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~node, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  labs(
    title = "Extended network nodes after nonparanormal transformation",
    subtitle = "The downstream climate_behavior node is transformed together with the attitude nodes",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Count"
  )
```

::: callout-note
These plots are diagnostic rather than substantive. The first shows the transformed distributions for the main retained belief-network nodes; the second shows the corresponding transformed distributions in the extended dataset, including climate_behavior.

This makes clear that `climate_behavior` is treated consistently with the other nodes in the extended Gaussian graphical model: it is entered as the same person-level composite, then transformed using the same nonparanormal procedure before network estimation.
:::

## 6.3 Main network: retained attitude and context nodes

```{r network-main, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
network_main <- estimateNetwork(
  df_net_main,
  default   = "EBICglasso",
  tuning    = 0.5,
  corMethod = "cor"
)

layout_main <- qgraph::averageLayout(getWmat(network_main))

plot(
  network_main,
  layout    = layout_main,
  labels    = node_labels[main_nodes],
  color     = node_colors[main_nodes],
  theme     = "colorblind",
  vsize     = 14,
  label.cex = 0.8,
  title     = "Main belief network",
  title.cex = 1.2,
  mar       = c(3, 3, 6, 3)
)
```

```{r network-main-edges}
edge_table_from_W <- function(W) {
  idx <- which(upper.tri(W) & W != 0, arr.ind = TRUE)

  if (nrow(idx) == 0) {
    return(tibble::tibble(
      from = character(),
      to = character(),
      weight = numeric(),
      abs_weight = numeric()
    ))
  }

  tibble::tibble(
    from   = rownames(W)[idx[, 1]],
    to     = colnames(W)[idx[, 2]],
    weight = W[idx]
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      abs_weight = abs(weight),
      weight     = round(weight, 3),
      abs_weight = round(abs_weight, 3)
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(abs_weight))
}

get_edge_weight <- function(tbl, a, b) {
  row <- tbl[(tbl$from == a & tbl$to == b) | (tbl$from == b & tbl$to == a), ]
  if (nrow(row) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  row$weight[1]
}

W_main <- network_main$graph
edge_table_main <- edge_table_from_W(W_main)
edge_table_main
```

The main Gaussian graphical model remains fairly dense after regularization: 24 of the 28 possible edges are retained. This means the final node set still behaves as a strongly interconnected between-person climate-attitude field rather than as a collection of near-independent domains. At the same time, the retained edges are not all equally strong, so the graph still reveals a meaningful conditional structure inside that broader shared field.

The strongest unique association in the main network is between `harm_present` and `harm_future` (`r sprintf("weight = %.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "harm_present", "harm_future"))`). This is substantively important. Even after controlling for all other retained nodes, present and future harm remain tightly linked, suggesting that these two composites are not merely correlated because both belong to a general pro-climate attitude factor. Rather, they still form the clearest residual backbone of the final belief network. The next strongest edge is between `policy_support` and `trust_science` (`r sprintf("weight = %.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "policy_support", "trust_science"))`), indicating that support for concrete climate policy and endorsement of expert-guided response remain closely connected once the rest of the system is partialled out.

`belief_concern` appears to play an important bridging role in the main graph. It retains specific links to `harm_present` (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "belief_concern", "harm_present"))`), `harm_future` (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "belief_concern", "harm_future"))`), `trust_science` (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "belief_concern", "trust_science"))`), and `policy_support` (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "belief_concern", "policy_support"))`). This pattern suggests that the belief/concern node sits between the harm-perception side of the system and the response/policy side, rather than collapsing entirely into either one. In other words, once the broader common climate-attitude variance is controlled, endorsement and concern still function as a meaningful connector across the network.

`social_norms` is also not simply absorbed into the shared climate-attitude field. Its clearest residual tie is to `trust_science` (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "social_norms", "trust_science"))`), with a smaller but still retained link to `policy_support` (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "social_norms", "policy_support"))`). That makes the norm node interpretable as part of the response-facing side of the network rather than as part of the harm backbone. This is useful for the later intervention question: norms survive as a specific node with their own conditional placement, even in a dense system.

`weather_risk_prep` and `politics` look more peripheral than the core harm/policy/belief block. `weather_risk_prep` nevertheless retains interpretable links, especially to `harm_present` (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "weather_risk_prep", "harm_present"))`) and `belief_concern` (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_main, "weather_risk_prep", "belief_concern"))`), which is substantively coherent: personal exposure to weather risk aligns more closely with concrete harm salience than with abstract policy or norm positioning. `politics` remains in the graph, but visually and substantively it reads more as a background-context node than as one of the central structural anchors of the network.

## 6.4 Edge-accuracy bootstrap

```{r network-main-bootstrap}
set.seed(123)

boot_main <- bootnet::bootnet(
  network_main,
  nBoots     = 1000,
  type       = "nonparametric",
  statistics = "edge",
  verbose    = FALSE,
  nCores     = max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 1)
)
```

```{r network-main-bootstrap-plot, fig.height=6}
plot(boot_main, labels = FALSE, order = "sample", plot = "interval")
```

The bootstrap supports a cautious interpretation of the main graph. The point is not to make strong claims about node centrality rankings, but to check how precisely the retained edge weights are estimated. In that sense, the bootstrap is most informative about the overall backbone of the network: the largest edges are the most defensible to describe, whereas smaller peripheral edges should be treated more tentatively. The practical implication is that the harm backbone, the policy–response link, and the main bridging role of `belief_concern` are the most interpretable parts of the graph, while fine-grained differences among weaker edges should not be overread.

## 6.5 Extended network: adding downstream climate behavior

```{r network-extended, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
network_ext <- estimateNetwork(
  df_net_ext,
  default   = "EBICglasso",
  tuning    = 0.5,
  corMethod = "cor"
)

layout_ext <- qgraph::averageLayout(getWmat(network_ext))

plot(
  network_ext,
  layout    = layout_ext,
  labels    = node_labels[extended_nodes],
  color     = node_colors[extended_nodes],
  theme     = "colorblind",
  vsize     = 14,
  label.cex = 0.75,
  title     = "Extended network — attitudes and downstream behavior",
  title.cex = 1.1,
  mar       = c(3, 3, 6, 3)
)
```

```{r network-extended-edges}
W_ext <- network_ext$graph
edge_table_ext <- edge_table_from_W(W_ext)
edge_table_ext
```

Adding `climate_behavior` does not fundamentally reorganize the attitudinal network. The same two core links remain dominant in the extended graph: `harm_present`–`harm_future` is again the strongest edge (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_ext, "harm_present", "harm_future"))`), and `policy_support`–`trust_science` remains second (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_ext, "policy_support", "trust_science"))`). This is important because it shows that the downstream behavior node does not replace or distort the main structure; instead, it attaches to a network whose backbone is already well defined.

The most notable behavior-related finding is that `weather_risk_prep` has the strongest specific connection to `climate_behavior` (`r sprintf("%.3f", get_edge_weight(edge_table_ext, "weather_risk_prep", "climate_behavior"))`). In fact, this is the only behavior edge that appears among the ten strongest edges in the extended network. That suggests that, once the stable attitude system is conditioned on itself, later climate-related behavior is linked most specifically to concrete weather-risk orientation rather than to the general pro-climate field in an undifferentiated way. This is substantively plausible, especially because the downstream behavior composite includes not only mitigation-type actions but also more protective or adaptation-like actions.

At the same time, `climate_behavior` sits at the edge of the graph rather than at its center. That is the expected pattern for a downstream outcome node. The extended network therefore should not be read as saying that behavior is just another interchangeable attitude indicator. Rather, it suggests that later behavior retains at least one specific conditional connection to the stable belief system, but remains structurally more peripheral than the core attitudinal nodes. Any additional behavior edges that survive are weaker than the main within-attitude edges and should be interpreted accordingly.

## 6.6 Network-estimation summary

The GGM refines the correlation matrix rather than overturning it. The retained nodes still form a dense positive climate-attitude field, but once shared variance is partialled out the residual structure is not uniform. Three features stand out. First, `harm_present` and `harm_future` form the clearest residual backbone of the system. Second, `policy_support`, `trust_science`, and `social_norms` define a more response-facing cluster. Third, `belief_concern` occupies a bridging position between the harm side and the response/policy side of the network. By contrast, `politics` and `weather_risk_prep` are more peripheral, although `weather_risk_prep` still retains interpretable ties to the harm side of the graph.

In the extended network, the same backbone remains visible in the wave-5 subsample, and `climate_behavior` attaches most clearly to `weather_risk_prep`. This is substantively plausible because the behavioral composite mixes mitigation-type actions with more protective or adaptation-like actions. The network analysis therefore does not imply that behavior is simply another interchangeable attitude indicator. Instead, it suggests that later behavior retains a small number of specific conditional links to the stable belief system while remaining structurally more peripheral than the core attitude nodes. These results are descriptive rather than causal: the GGM identifies which associations remain uniquely visible once the broader shared climate-attitude field is partialled out.

# 7. Causal discovery

The causal-discovery stage is used here as a hypothesis-generating tool rather than as a procedure expected to recover a unique true causal graph from observational survey composites. FCI is treated as the primary analysis because latent common causes are plausible in this setting, whereas PC-stable serves as a sensitivity analysis under causal sufficiency. The main empirical goal is therefore to identify which adjacencies recur robustly across algorithms, alpha thresholds, and bootstrap resamples, and only secondarily to examine whether a smaller subset of orientations appears stable enough to inform later modeling. Accordingly, adjacency is interpreted more confidently than direction throughout this section.

Constraint-based causal discovery is applied to the nonparanormal-transformed composite scores using two complementary algorithms:

- **FCI** as the primary analysis, because it allows for latent confounding and returns a PAG.
- **PC-stable** as a sensitivity analysis, because it assumes causal sufficiency and returns a CPDAG.

Both algorithms are run at `α = 0.05` and `α = 0.01`. The stricter threshold is useful because it yields a sparser graph and provides a more conservative visual reference, but neither threshold is treated as definitive on its own. A nonparametric bootstrap with `N = 2500` resamples is then run separately at both alpha levels. The bootstrap is used to summarize how often each adjacency and each endpoint mark recurs across resamples. These proportions are examined first within each alpha level and then after pooling raw counts across both alpha levels. The resulting pooled summaries are used to visualize a dominant-mark backbone, not to claim that every displayed orientation is equally well identified.

::: callout-important
**On interpreting PAGs and CPDAGs.**

A **PAG** from FCI allows for latent common causes. Its endpoint marks distinguish stronger from weaker orientation statements:

| Mark pair | Interpretation |
|-----------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| Tail — Arrowhead (`X → Y`) | `X` is an ancestor of `Y`; no latent common cause is needed for that edge |
| Arrowhead — Arrowhead (`X ↔ Y`) | Compatible with latent common cause |
| Circle — Arrowhead (`X ○→ Y`) | `Y` is not an ancestor of `X`, but the status of `X` remains uncertain |
| Circle — Circle (`X ○—○ Y`) | Orientation unresolved |

A **CPDAG** from PC assumes no latent common causes. Directed edges are orientation-invariant within the equivalence class, whereas undirected edges remain unresolved. Because these survey composites are likely to share unmeasured determinants, PC is treated here as a sensitivity analysis rather than as the primary causal representation.
:::

## 7.1 Setup

The causal-discovery analysis is conducted on the eight retained attitude/context nodes used in the main GGM: `belief_concern`, `harm_present`, `harm_future`, `policy_support`, `trust_science`, `social_norms`, `politics`, and `weather_risk_prep`.

```{r causal-setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(pcalg)
  library(graph)
  library(Rgraphviz)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggraph)
  library(tidygraph)
  library(qgraph)
})

node_order_cd <- c(
  "belief_concern", "harm_present", "harm_future",
  "policy_support", "trust_science", "social_norms",
  "politics", "weather_risk_prep"
)

agg_data <- df_net_main[, node_order_cd]
p        <- length(node_order_cd)

suffStat_gauss <- list(C = cor(agg_data), n = nrow(agg_data))

abbr <- c(
  belief_concern       = "BC",
  harm_present         = "HP",
  harm_future          = "HF",
  policy_support       = "PS",
  trust_science         = "TS",
  social_norms         = "SN",
  politics             = "POL",
  weather_risk_prep    = "WR"
)

cat("N =", nrow(agg_data), " p =", p, "\n")
cat("Nodes:", paste(node_order_cd, collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

```{r plot-helpers}
plotAG <- function(amat, title_text = NULL, save_path = NULL, layout_save_path = NULL) {
  # v2 (2026-09-05): pretty node labels/colors (reuses node_labels/node_colors
  # from Section 1) instead of raw variable names, plus an optional save_path
  # so this auto-exports a fresh PNG every time it's knit -- Panel B of
  # Figure 3 previously had to be hand-exported, which is why it
  # went stale (still showed the pre-ew6-removal variable set) after the
  # ew6 exclusion. Knitting through Section 7 now regenerates the PNG
  # automatically, so it can never drift from the current node set again.
  #
  # v3 (2026-09-05): added layout_save_path so the SCM diagram
  # (07_figure5_scm_hierarchical_v3.R) can share this graph's node layout and
  # colors instead of hand-tuning qgraph's curve/label parameters by eye --
  # a real graph-layout algorithm (Rgraphviz's layoutGraph(), used here)
  # inherently avoids node overlaps for whatever edge set it's given, which
  # is a lot more reliable than eyeballing curvature by hand. When
  # layout_save_path is set, the (x, y) position
  # Rgraphviz computed for every node is written out as a plain CSV that
  # 07_figure5_scm_hierarchical_v3.R now reads and reuses (matched by node
  # name, not row order) instead of its own fixed_layout_matrix() coordinates.
  g   <- as(amat, "graphNEL")
  nn  <- nodes(g); p <- numNodes(g); ne <- numEdges(g)
  ah  <- at <- vector("list", ne); ln <- character(ne)
  sym <- amat
  sym[sym == 1] <- "odot"; sym[sym == 2] <- "vee"
  sym[sym == 3] <- "none"; sym[sym == 4] <- "tee"
  iE <- 0
  for (i in 1:(p - 1)) for (j in (i + 1):p) {
    x <- nn[i]; y <- nn[j]
    if (sym[x, y] != 0) {
      iE <- iE + 1
      ah[[iE]] <- sym[x, y]; at[[iE]] <- sym[y, x]
      ln[[iE]] <- paste0(x, "~", y)
    }
  }
  names(ah) <- names(at) <- ln
  edgeRenderInfo(g) <- list(arrowhead = ah, arrowtail = at,
                            lwd = 2.1, col = "#4A4A4A")
  # label/fontsize/cex are set BEFORE layoutGraph() because layoutGraph uses
  # them to size each node's bounding box -- they need to be inputs to the
  # layout step, not just outputs of it.
  nodeRenderInfo(g) <- list(
    label    = setNames(node_labels[nn], nn),
    fontsize = 15,
    cex      = 1
  )
  graph.par(list(nodes = list(cex = 1)))
  g_laid_out <- Rgraphviz::layoutGraph(g)
  # FIX 2026-09-05: fill/col/lwd were originally set in the same block above
  # (before layoutGraph()) and silently did nothing -- the rendered PNG came
  # out with plain white nodes despite node_colors being passed in.
  # layoutGraph() resets purely-cosmetic render attributes it doesn't need
  # for layout (fill isn't a layout input the way label/fontsize are), so
  # anything color-related has to be (re-)applied to the LAID-OUT graph,
  # after layoutGraph(), not before it.
  nodeRenderInfo(g_laid_out) <- list(
    fill = setNames(node_colors[nn], nn),
    col  = "#4A4A4A",
    lwd  = 1.4
  )
  if (!is.null(layout_save_path)) {
    # NOTE 2026-09-05: getNodeXY() only works on the older "Ragraph" objects
    # returned by Rgraphviz::agopen() -- it errored here ("unable to find an
    # inherited method ... for signature object = 'graphNEL'") because
    # layoutGraph()/renderGraph() (the API this function actually uses)
    # returns a graphNEL with layout info attached via nodeRenderInfo()
    # instead. That's where the computed (x, y) positions actually live.
    nri <- nodeRenderInfo(g_laid_out)  # unprefixed, same as the nodeRenderInfo(g) <- ... setter above
    layout_df <- data.frame(name = names(nri$nodeX), x = unname(nri$nodeX), y = unname(nri$nodeY))
    dir.create(dirname(layout_save_path), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
    write.csv(layout_df, layout_save_path, row.names = FALSE)
    cat("Wrote node layout (for reuse in the SCM figure) to", layout_save_path, "\n")
  }
  render_once <- function() {
    par(mar = c(1, 1, 6, 1))
    Rgraphviz::renderGraph(g_laid_out)
    if (!is.null(title_text))
      title(main = title_text, cex.main = 1.15, line = 4, font.main = 2)
  }
  if (!is.null(save_path)) {
    dir.create(dirname(save_path), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
    grDevices::png(save_path, width = 1500, height = 1500, res = 220, bg = "white")
    render_once()
    grDevices::dev.off()
  }
  render_once()
}

plotPC <- function(amat, title_text = NULL) {
  g  <- as(amat, "graphNEL")
  nn <- nodes(g); p <- numNodes(g); ne <- numEdges(g)
  ah <- at <- vector("list", ne); ln <- character(ne)
  iE <- 0
  for (i in 1:(p-1)) for (j in (i+1):p) {
    # Skip if no edge in either direction
    if (amat[i,j] == 0 && amat[j,i] == 0) next
    iE <- iE + 1
    if (amat[i,j] == 1 && amat[j,i] == 1) {
      # Undirected
      ah[[iE]] <- "none"; at[[iE]] <- "none"
    } else if (amat[i,j] == 1 && amat[j,i] == 0) {
      # i -> j
      ah[[iE]] <- "vee";  at[[iE]] <- "none"
    } else {
      # j -> i
      ah[[iE]] <- "none"; at[[iE]] <- "vee"
    }
    ln[[iE]] <- paste0(nn[i], "~", nn[j])
  }
  ah <- ah[seq_len(iE)]; at <- at[seq_len(iE)]; ln <- ln[seq_len(iE)]
  names(ah) <- names(at) <- ln
  edgeRenderInfo(g) <- list(arrowhead = ah, arrowtail = at)
  graph.par(list(nodes = list(cex = 1)))
  Rgraphviz::renderGraph(Rgraphviz::layoutGraph(g))
  if (!is.null(title_text))
    title(main = title_text, cex.main = 1.1, line = 3)
}

decode_pag_edges <- function(amat, nms) {
  p <- nrow(amat); rows <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(p - 1)) for (j in (i + 1):p) {
    if (amat[i,j] == 0 && amat[j,i] == 0) next
    m_ij <- switch(as.character(amat[i,j]),"1"="o","2"=">","3"="-","0"="?")
    m_ji <- switch(as.character(amat[j,i]),"1"="o","2"=">","3"="-","0"="?")
    lbl <- dplyr::case_when(
      amat[i,j]==2 & amat[j,i]==3 ~
        paste0(nms[i]," \u2192 ",nms[j]," (ancestor, no latent)"),
      amat[j,i]==2 & amat[i,j]==3 ~
        paste0(nms[j]," \u2192 ",nms[i]," (ancestor, no latent)"),
      amat[i,j]==2 & amat[j,i]==2 ~ "Bidirected (latent common cause)",
      amat[i,j]==1 & amat[j,i]==1 ~ "Circle-circle (complete uncertainty)",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
    rows[[length(rows)+1]] <- data.frame(
      edge = paste0(nms[i]," ",m_ji,"--",m_ij," ",nms[j]),
      type = lbl, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }
  dplyr::bind_rows(rows)
}
```

## 7.2 Single-run graphs at `α = 0.05` and `α = 0.01`

```{r fci-05, fig.height=6, fig.width=6}
fci_05 <- fci(suffStat = suffStat_gauss, indepTest = gaussCItest,
              alpha = 0.05, labels = node_order_cd, verbose = FALSE)
plotAG(fci_05@amat, "FCI — PAG (\u03b1 = 0.05)",
       save_path = "figures/fci_pag_alpha05.png")
```

```{r fci-01, fig.height=6, fig.width=6}
fci_01 <- fci(suffStat = suffStat_gauss, indepTest = gaussCItest,
              alpha = 0.01, labels = node_order_cd, verbose = FALSE)
plotAG(fci_01@amat, "FCI — PAG (\u03b1 = 0.01)",
       save_path = "figures/fci_pag_alpha01.png")
```

The single-run causal graphs should be read conservatively. Their main value is not that they identify one clean causal graph, but that they reveal which parts of the climate-attitude system admit a reasonably stable causal ordering and which parts remain unresolved once latent confounding is allowed. In this dataset, the clearest structure appears at `α = 0.01`, where the FCI PAG recovers a compact backbone centered on `belief_concern`, `harm_present`, `harm_future`, `policy_support`, and `social_norms`.

At the level of formal PAG interpretation, the strongest directional information in the FCI graph is concentrated in that backbone. `belief_concern` carries tail-arrowhead marks toward `harm_present`, `harm_future`, and `policy_support`, which means it is estimated as an ancestor of those nodes in every MAG compatible with the data. `harm_future` is likewise estimated as an ancestor of `harm_present` and `policy_support`, and `harm_present` is estimated as an ancestor of `social_norms`. These are the clearest directional statements supported by the current PAG.

By contrast, several other edges are not cleanly orientable. The links from `belief_concern` and `harm_present` into `trust_science`, `politics`, and `weather_risk_prep` are bidirected in the decoded FCI output, which should be interpreted as compatibility with latent common causes rather than as a methodological failure. In other words, these nodes are clearly part of the same conditional-dependence structure, but their causal ordering is not identified from these data. That is exactly the kind of uncertainty the PAG is meant to display.

PC-stable does not overturn this picture. Its main contribution is that it recovers the same adjacency skeleton at both thresholds, even though it operates under the stronger assumption of causal sufficiency and returns a CPDAG rather than a PAG. So the single-run graphs already suggest an important distinction: the adjacency backbone is relatively stable, whereas the orientation pattern is only partially identified and should be treated as hypothesis-generating.

```{r pc-05, fig.height=6, fig.width=6}
pc_05 <- pc(suffStat = suffStat_gauss, indepTest = gaussCItest,
            alpha = 0.05, labels = node_order_cd,
            skel.method = "stable", verbose = FALSE)
pc_amat_05 <- as(pc_05@graph, "matrix")
par(mar = c(1,1,4,1))
plotPC(pc_amat_05, "PC-stable — CPDAG (\u03b1 = 0.05)")
```

```{r pc-01, fig.height=6, fig.width=6}
pc_01 <- pc(suffStat = suffStat_gauss, indepTest = gaussCItest,
            alpha = 0.01, labels = node_order_cd,
            skel.method = "stable", verbose = FALSE)
pc_amat_01 <- as(pc_01@graph, "matrix")
par(mar = c(1,1,4,1))
plotPC(pc_amat_01, "PC-stable — CPDAG (\u03b1 = 0.01)")
```

The FCI PAG at α = 0.01 recovers a compact structure anchored by a **belief–harm–policy backbone**: `belief_concern` carries tail-arrowhead marks toward `harm_present`, `harm_future`, and `policy_support`; `harm_future` is a consistent ancestor of `harm_present` and `policy_support`; `harm_present` is a consistent ancestor of `social_norms`. The edges linking `belief_concern` and `harm_present` to `trust_science`, `politics`, and `weather_risk_prep` are bidirected — latent common causes, not directionalisable from these data. PC-stable recovers the same skeleton at both thresholds.

## 7.3 Bootstrap endpoint-mark proportion matrices

To assess stability more systematically, a nonparametric bootstrap is run separately at `α = 0.05` and `α = 0.01` for both FCI and PC. In each bootstrap resample, the relevant discovery algorithm is re-estimated on the resampled data. For every ordered node pair `(i, j)`, the code records the mark at the `j` endpoint. For FCI, the possible marks are `N` (no edge), `o`, `>`, and `-`. For PC, the possible marks are `N`, `-`, and `>`. Repeating this across 2500 resamples yields, for each alpha level and each algorithm, an empirical proportion distribution over endpoint marks.

These proportions are first displayed separately for `α = 0.05` and `α = 0.01`. The raw bootstrap counts are then pooled across both alpha levels and divided by `2 × 2500 = 5000` to obtain combined endpoint-mark proportions. This pooling step is descriptive: it summarizes what recurs across the two thresholds rather than privileging one of them absolutely. The pooled “stable graph” is then constructed as a dominant-mark summary. In practice, an ordered endpoint is shown only if absence (`N`) is not the dominant pooled mark; among the remaining marks, the dominant non-absence mark is displayed. These pooled stable graphs are therefore best understood as visual summaries of recurring structure, not as fully identified causal solutions.

```{r bootstrap}
# ── Bootstrap ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
library(furrr); library(future)
n_cores <- max(1L, parallelly::availableCores() - 1L)
plan(multisession, workers = n_cores)

n_boot    <- 2500
alphas    <- c("0.05" = 0.05, "0.01" = 0.01)
fci_marks <- c("N", "o", ">", "-")
pc_marks  <- c("N", "-", ">")

run_one <- function(b, data, nms, alpha) {
  p      <- length(nms)
  idx    <- sample(nrow(data), replace = TRUE)
  suff_b <- list(C = cor(as.matrix(data[idx, ])), n = length(idx))
  fci_arr <- array(0L, dim = c(p, p, 4L))
  pc_arr  <- array(0L, dim = c(p, p, 3L))

  tryCatch({
    fci_b <- pcalg::fci(
      suffStat = suff_b, indepTest = pcalg::gaussCItest,
      alpha = alpha, labels = nms, verbose = FALSE)
    am <- fci_b@amat
    for (i in seq_len(p)) for (j in seq_len(p)) {
      if (i == j) next
      slot <- am[i, j] + 1L
      fci_arr[i, j, slot] <- fci_arr[i, j, slot] + 1L
    }
  }, error = function(e) NULL)

  tryCatch({
    pc_b <- pcalg::pc(
      suffStat = suff_b, indepTest = pcalg::gaussCItest,
      alpha = alpha, labels = nms,
      skel.method = "stable", verbose = FALSE)
    am <- as(pc_b@graph, "matrix")
    for (i in seq_len(p)) for (j in seq_len(p)) {
      if (i == j) next
      slot <- if      (am[i,j]==0L && am[j,i]==0L) 1L
              else if (am[i,j]==1L && am[j,i]==1L) 2L
              else if (am[i,j]==1L && am[j,i]==0L) 3L
              else if (am[i,j]==0L && am[j,i]==1L) 2L
              else                                  1L
      pc_arr[i, j, slot] <- pc_arr[i, j, slot] + 1L
    }
  }, error = function(e) NULL)

  list(fci = fci_arr, pc = pc_arr)
}

set.seed(42)
results <- list()
for (alph in names(alphas)) {
  cat("Bootstrap \u03b1 =", alph, "\n")
  results[[alph]] <- furrr::future_map(
    seq_len(n_boot), run_one,
    data  = agg_data, nms = node_order_cd,
    alpha = alphas[[alph]],
    .options  = furrr::furrr_options(seed = TRUE),
    .progress = TRUE)
}
plan(sequential)

# ── Accumulate raw counts ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
mark_props <- list()
for (alph in names(alphas)) {
  fci_c <- array(0L, dim = c(p, p, 4L),
                 dimnames = list(node_order_cd, node_order_cd, fci_marks))
  pc_c  <- array(0L, dim = c(p, p, 3L),
                 dimnames = list(node_order_cd, node_order_cd, pc_marks))
  for (res in results[[alph]]) {
    if (is.null(res)) next
    fci_c <- fci_c + res$fci
    pc_c  <- pc_c  + res$pc
  }
  # Sanity check
  fci_sums <- apply(fci_c, c(1,2), sum); diag(fci_sums) <- n_boot
  pc_sums  <- apply(pc_c,  c(1,2), sum); diag(pc_sums)  <- n_boot
  if (any(abs(fci_sums - n_boot) > 1))
    warning(sprintf("Alpha %s: FCI cell sums deviate from %d", alph, n_boot))
  if (any(abs(pc_sums  - n_boot) > 1))
    warning(sprintf("Alpha %s: PC cell sums deviate from %d",  alph, n_boot))

  # Store raw counts (not proportions) so we can pool later
  mark_props[[alph]] <- list(
    fci       = fci_c / n_boot,
    pc        = pc_c  / n_boot,
    fci_counts = fci_c,
    pc_counts  = pc_c
  )
}

# ── Combined: pool raw counts across both alphas, divide by 2*n_boot ─────────
# Each cell proportion = (count at α=0.05 + count at α=0.01) / 2000.
# A mark scoring 0.80 appeared in ≥80% of all 2000 resamples combined.
fci_props_combined <- (mark_props[["0.05"]]$fci_counts +
                        mark_props[["0.01"]]$fci_counts) / (2 * n_boot)
pc_props_combined  <- (mark_props[["0.05"]]$pc_counts  +
                        mark_props[["0.01"]]$pc_counts)  / (2 * n_boot)

# Give dimnames
dimnames(fci_props_combined) <- list(node_order_cd, node_order_cd, fci_marks)
dimnames(pc_props_combined)  <- list(node_order_cd, node_order_cd, pc_marks)

# Sanity: cells should sum to 1
fci_cs <- apply(fci_props_combined, c(1,2), sum); diag(fci_cs) <- 1
pc_cs  <- apply(pc_props_combined,  c(1,2), sum); diag(pc_cs)  <- 1
if (any(abs(fci_cs - 1) > 0.01)) warning("FCI combined props don't sum to 1")
if (any(abs(pc_cs  - 1) > 0.01)) warning("PC combined props don't sum to 1")

cat("Bootstrap complete.", n_boot, "resamples per alpha threshold.",
    "Proportions pooled across both thresholds for summary displays,",
    "not treated as", 2*n_boot, "independent draws.\n")
```

```{r plot-mark-fn}
# ── Plot function ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
display_label <- function(mark) {
  dplyr::case_when(mark == "-" ~ "\u2014", TRUE ~ mark)
}

plot_mark_matrix <- function(props, marks, title, subtitle,
                              show_legend = FALSE) {   # legend off by default

  base_cols <- c("N"="#aaaaaa","o"="#2e7d8e",">"="#1b5e38","-"="#b5534a")
  alpha_floor <- 0.15
  display <- c("N"="N","o"="o",">"=">","-"="\u2014")

  cells <- expand.grid(i=seq_len(p), j=seq_len(p),
                       stringsAsFactors=FALSE) |>
    dplyr::filter(i != j) |>
    dplyr::mutate(row_node=node_order_cd[i], col_node=node_order_cd[j]) |>
    dplyr::rowwise() |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      dominant = marks[which.max(props[i,j,])],
      dom_prop = max(props[i,j,]),
      label = {
        vals <- props[i,j,]; keep <- vals > 0.04
        if (any(keep))
          paste0(display[marks[keep]], ": ",
                 sprintf("%.2f", vals[keep]), collapse="\n")
        else ""
      },
      fill = adjustcolor(base_cols[dominant],
                         alpha.f = alpha_floor + (1-alpha_floor)*dom_prop),
      text_col = dplyr::if_else(dom_prop < 0.30 | dominant=="N",
                                "#333333","white")
    ) |> dplyr::ungroup()

  diag_df <- data.frame(node=node_order_cd, label=abbr[node_order_cd])

  legend_df <- data.frame(
    x     = c(1,2,3,4),
    label = c("N = absent","o = circle","> = arrowhead","\u2014 = tail"),
    fill  = unname(base_cols[c("N","o",">","-")])
  )

  plt <- ggplot() +
    geom_tile(data=cells, aes(x=col_node,y=row_node,fill=fill),
              color="white", linewidth=0.8) +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    geom_text(data=cells,
              aes(x=col_node,y=row_node,label=label,color=text_col),
              size=2.2, fontface="bold", lineheight=1.1) +
    scale_color_identity() +
    geom_text(data=diag_df, aes(x=node,y=node,label=label),
              size=3, color="grey30", fontface="bold") +
    scale_x_discrete(limits=node_order_cd, labels=abbr[node_order_cd],
                     position="top") +
    scale_y_discrete(limits=rev(node_order_cd),
                     labels=abbr[rev(node_order_cd)]) +
    labs(title=title, subtitle=subtitle) +
    theme_minimal(base_size=13) +
    theme(axis.title=element_blank(),
          axis.text.x=element_text(face="bold",size=9),
          axis.text.y=element_text(face="bold",size=9),
          panel.grid=element_blank(),
          plot.title=element_text(face="bold",size=11),
          plot.subtitle=element_text(size=8,color="grey50",lineheight=1.3),
          plot.margin=margin(5,5,5,5))
  
  if (show_legend) {
    plt <- plt +
      annotate("tile", x=c(1.5, 3.5, 5.5, 7.5), y=rep(-0.7, 4),
               width=1.6, height=0.45, fill=legend_df$fill, alpha=0.9) +
      annotate("text", x=c(1.5, 3.5, 5.5, 7.5), y=rep(-0.7, 4),
               label=legend_df$label, size=2.6, colour="white", fontface="bold") +
      annotate("text", x=0.3, y=-0.7, label="Mark\ntype:",
               hjust=1, size=2.4, colour="grey40") +
      coord_cartesian(clip="off") +
      theme(plot.margin=margin(5,5,25,5))
  }
  
  plt
}

# ── Standalone legend plot ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
make_legend_plot <- function() {
  base_cols <- c("N"="#aaaaaa","o"="#2e7d8e",">"="#1b5e38","-"="#b5534a")
  legend_df <- data.frame(
    x     = 1:4,
    label = c("N = absent","o = circle","\u2265 = arrowhead","\u2014 = tail"),
    fill  = unname(base_cols[c("N","o",">","-")])
  )
  ggplot(legend_df, aes(x=x, y=1)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill=fill), width=0.9, height=0.7, alpha=0.9) +
    geom_text(aes(label=label), colour="white", fontface="bold", size=3.2) +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    annotate("text", x=0.35, y=1, label="Mark type:",
             hjust=1, size=3, colour="grey40") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,5)) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(plot.margin=margin(2,2,2,2))
}
```

```{r}
fci_non_n <- c("o", ">", "-")
pc_non_n  <- c("-", ">")

# ── FCI amat ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fci_amat_stable <- matrix(0L, nrow=p, ncol=p,
                           dimnames=list(node_order_cd, node_order_cd))

for (i in seq_len(p)) {
  for (j in seq_len(p)) {
    if (i == j) next
    # Only draw edge if N is not the dominant mark
    if (fci_props_combined[i,j,"N"] >= 0.5) next

    dom_mark <- fci_non_n[which.max(fci_props_combined[i, j, fci_non_n])]
    fci_amat_stable[i, j] <- switch(dom_mark,
                                     "o" = 1L, ">" = 2L, "-" = 3L, 0L)
  }
}

# ── PC amat ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pc_amat_stable <- matrix(0L, nrow=p, ncol=p,
                          dimnames=list(node_order_cd, node_order_cd))

for (i in seq_len(p)) {
  for (j in seq_len(p)) {
    if (i == j) next
    if (pc_props_combined[i,j,"N"] >= 0.5) next

    dom_mark <- pc_non_n[which.max(pc_props_combined[i, j, pc_non_n])]
    if (dom_mark == ">") {
      pc_amat_stable[i, j] <- 1L
    } else {
      pc_amat_stable[j, i] <- 1L
    }
  }
}
```

**Bootstrap summary.** The bootstrap strengthens the adjacency conclusions more than the orientation conclusions. Across both algorithms and both alpha thresholds, the results support a robust conditional-dependence backbone linking `belief_concern`, the two harm nodes, `policy_support`, `trust_science`, `social_norms`, `politics`, and `weather_risk_prep`. By contrast, endpoint marks are less stable, so most directional conclusions remain provisional. The causal-discovery stage therefore supports a strong statement about which nodes belong to the same robust conditional-dependence structure, but only a narrower statement about how those nodes are ordered. For that reason, the strongest empirical result of this section is the backbone itself, not a fully resolved directed graph.

## 7.4 Extended analysis — downstream climate_behavior

The extended analysis adds `climate_behavior` as a downstream wave-5 outcome. The same overall discovery pipeline is repeated: single-run graphs at both alpha levels, bootstrap endpoint-mark proportions at both alpha levels, pooled proportions across both alpha levels, and a dominant-mark summary graph.

Here, however, the analysis also encodes measurement order as background knowledge so that the wave-5 behavior node is not allowed to act as a cause of the earlier attitude/context nodes. In the FCI analysis this is done through the JCI formulation, treating the earlier attitude/context nodes as context variables relative to `climate_behavior`. In the PC analysis this is done by adding background knowledge only where an undirected edge between an attitude node and `climate_behavior` is present. This means the extended discovery stage does not attempt to infer whether behavior causes earlier attitudes; that possibility is excluded by design because the temporal ordering of measurement already places the attitude/context system upstream of the wave-5 behavior outcome.

```{r ext-setup}
node_order_ext <- c(node_order_cd, "climate_behavior")
p_ext          <- length(node_order_ext)
abbr_ext       <- c(abbr, climate_behavior = "CB")

agg_ext <- df_net_ext[, node_order_ext]

suffStat_ext <- list(
  C = cor(agg_ext, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"),
  n = nrow(agg_ext)
)

# Attitude nodes are context (upstream) variables for FCI-JCI
context_idx <- which(node_order_ext %in% node_order_cd)

# Background knowledge for PC: every attitude node -> CB
bg_x <- node_order_cd
bg_y <- rep("climate_behavior", length(node_order_cd))

cat("Extended nodes:", paste(node_order_ext, collapse=", "), "\n")
cat("N =", nrow(agg_ext), "\n")
```

```{r ext-bootstrap}
library(furrr); library(future)
n_cores <- max(1L, parallelly::availableCores() - 1L)
plan(multisession, workers = n_cores)

fci_marks_ext <- c("N","o",">","-")
pc_marks_ext  <- c("N","-",">")

run_one_ext <- function(b, data, nms, alpha, ctx_idx) {
  p      <- length(nms)
  idx    <- sample(nrow(data), replace=TRUE)
  suff_b <- list(C=cor(as.matrix(data[idx,])), n=length(idx))
  fci_arr <- array(0L, dim=c(p,p,4L))
  pc_arr  <- array(0L, dim=c(p,p,3L))

  # ── FCI ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  tryCatch({
    fci_b <- pcalg::fci(
      suffStat=suff_b, indepTest=pcalg::gaussCItest,
      alpha=alpha, labels=nms,
      contextVars=ctx_idx, jci="1",
      selectionBias=FALSE, verbose=FALSE)
    am <- fci_b@amat
    for (i in seq_len(p)) for (j in seq_len(p)) {
      if (i==j) next
      slot <- am[i,j]+1L
      fci_arr[i,j,slot] <- fci_arr[i,j,slot]+1L
    }
  }, error=function(e) NULL)
  
  # ── PC + background knowledge ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  tryCatch({
    pc_b <- pcalg::pc(
      suffStat=suff_b, indepTest=pcalg::gaussCItest,
      alpha=alpha, labels=nms,
      skel.method="stable", verbose=FALSE)
    am <- as(pc_b@graph, "matrix")
    
    # Only orient undirected edges that actually exist towards CB
    att_nms <- nms[nms != "climate_behavior"]
    bg_pairs <- Filter(function(a)
      am[a,"climate_behavior"]==1 && am["climate_behavior",a]==1,
      att_nms)
    
    if (length(bg_pairs) > 0) {
      bg_result <- pcalg::addBgKnowledge(
        gInput = pc_b@graph,
        x      = bg_pairs,
        y      = rep("climate_behavior", length(bg_pairs)))
      am <- as(bg_result, "matrix")
    }
    
    for (i in seq_len(p)) for (j in seq_len(p)) {
      if (i==j) next
      slot <- if      (am[i,j]==0L && am[j,i]==0L) 1L
      else if (am[i,j]==1L && am[j,i]==1L) 2L
      else if (am[i,j]==1L && am[j,i]==0L) 3L
      else if (am[i,j]==0L && am[j,i]==1L) 2L
      else                                  1L
      pc_arr[i,j,slot] <- pc_arr[i,j,slot]+1L
    }
  }, error=function(e) NULL)
  
  list(fci=fci_arr, pc=pc_arr)
}

set.seed(42)
results_ext <- list()
for (alph in names(alphas)) {
  cat("Extended bootstrap \u03b1 =", alph, "\n")
  results_ext[[alph]] <- furrr::future_map(
    seq_len(n_boot), run_one_ext,
    data    = agg_ext,
    nms     = node_order_ext,
    alpha   = alphas[[alph]],
    ctx_idx = context_idx,
    .options  = furrr::furrr_options(seed=TRUE),
    .progress = TRUE)
}
plan(sequential)

# ── Accumulate ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
mark_props_ext <- list()
for (alph in names(alphas)) {
  fci_c <- array(0L, dim=c(p_ext,p_ext,4L),
                 dimnames=list(node_order_ext,node_order_ext,fci_marks_ext))
  pc_c  <- array(0L, dim=c(p_ext,p_ext,3L),
                 dimnames=list(node_order_ext,node_order_ext,pc_marks_ext))
  for (res in results_ext[[alph]]) {
    if (is.null(res)) next
    fci_c <- fci_c + res$fci
    pc_c  <- pc_c  + res$pc
  }
  mark_props_ext[[alph]] <- list(
    fci        = fci_c / n_boot,
    pc         = pc_c  / n_boot,
    fci_counts = fci_c,
    pc_counts  = pc_c)
}

# ── Pool across both alphas ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
fci_props_ext <- (mark_props_ext[["0.05"]]$fci_counts +
                   mark_props_ext[["0.01"]]$fci_counts) / (2*n_boot)
pc_props_ext  <- (mark_props_ext[["0.05"]]$pc_counts  +
                   mark_props_ext[["0.01"]]$pc_counts)  / (2*n_boot)

dimnames(fci_props_ext) <- list(node_order_ext, node_order_ext, fci_marks_ext)
dimnames(pc_props_ext)  <- list(node_order_ext, node_order_ext, pc_marks_ext)

# Persist the per-alpha (unpooled) mark proportions alongside the pooled summary.
# fci_props_ext.rds (pooled) already supports Table 2 / script 18; this additional
# object lets downstream scripts assess cross-alpha orientation consistency, which
# the pooled array cannot answer on its own (see r_patches/21_orientation_crossalpha_table.R).
dir.create("pipeline_outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(mark_props_ext, "pipeline_outputs/mark_props_ext_by_alpha.rds")

cat("Extended bootstrap complete.", n_boot,
    "resamples per alpha threshold, pooled across both for summary displays.\n")
cat("Per-alpha mark proportions saved to pipeline_outputs/mark_props_ext_by_alpha.rds\n")
```

```{r ext-plot-fn}
# Wrapper: swaps global p / node_order_cd / abbr for extended versions
plot_mark_matrix_ext <- function(props, marks, title, subtitle,
                                  show_legend=FALSE) {
  e <- globalenv()
  old_p   <- get("p",            envir=e)
  old_nms <- get("node_order_cd", envir=e)
  old_abb <- get("abbr",         envir=e)
  assign("p",            p_ext,          envir=e)
  assign("node_order_cd", node_order_ext, envir=e)
  assign("abbr",         abbr_ext,       envir=e)
  on.exit({
    assign("p",            old_p,   envir=e)
    assign("node_order_cd", old_nms, envir=e)
    assign("abbr",         old_abb, envir=e)
  })
  plot_mark_matrix(props, marks, title, subtitle, show_legend)
}
```

```{r ext-amats}
fci_non_n_e <- c("o",">","-")
pc_non_n_e  <- c("-",">")

# ── FCI extended amat ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fci_amat_ext <- matrix(0L, nrow=p_ext, ncol=p_ext,
                        dimnames=list(node_order_ext,node_order_ext))

for (i in seq_len(p_ext)) {
  for (j in seq_len(p_ext)) {
    if (i==j) next
    if (fci_props_ext[i,j,"N"] >= 0.5) next
    dom_mark <- fci_non_n_e[which.max(fci_props_ext[i,j,fci_non_n_e])]
    fci_amat_ext[i,j] <- switch(dom_mark,"o"=1L,">"=2L,"-"=3L,0L)
  }
}

# ── PC extended amat ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pc_amat_ext <- matrix(0L, nrow=p_ext, ncol=p_ext,
                       dimnames=list(node_order_ext,node_order_ext))

for (i in seq_len(p_ext-1)) {
  for (j in (i+1):p_ext) {
    inc <- ((1-pc_props_ext[i,j,"N"]) + (1-pc_props_ext[j,i,"N"])) / 2
    if (inc < 0.5) next

    ni <- node_order_ext[i]; nj <- node_order_ext[j]

    # CB always downstream
    if (nj == "climate_behavior") {
      pc_amat_ext[i,j] <- 1L; next
    }
    if (ni == "climate_behavior") {
      pc_amat_ext[j,i] <- 1L; next
    }

    # Attitude-attitude: dominant arrowhead direction wins
    arr_ij <- pc_props_ext[i,j,">"]
    arr_ji <- pc_props_ext[j,i,">"]
    if      (arr_ij > arr_ji + 0.10) { pc_amat_ext[i,j] <- 1L }
    else if (arr_ji > arr_ij + 0.10) { pc_amat_ext[j,i] <- 1L }
    else {
      pc_amat_ext[i,j] <- 1L
      pc_amat_ext[j,i] <- 1L
    }
  }
}
```

**Extended behavior summary.** In the extended analysis, the most robust behavior-adjacent nodes are `harm_present` and `weather_risk_prep`. These edges appear in both FCI and PC and therefore represent the strongest evidence for specific links between the earlier attitude/context system and later behavior. `social_norms` is more tentative: it appears in PC and in broader robustness summaries, but not as consistently in the stricter FCI result. The safest interpretation is therefore that later climate-related behavior is tied most robustly to present-harm salience and weather-risk perception, with `social_norms` remaining a plausible but weaker secondary candidate. Because `social_norms` is defined here by `cvcc4_should`, any possible downstream norm pathway should be interpreted as an **injunctive-norm** pathway, reflecting perceived normative obligation, rather than as evidence about descriptive expectations of what others will do. This pattern is also substantively coherent given that the behavioral composite includes both mitigation-type and more protective/adaptation-like actions.

## 7.5 Theory-augmented working SCM for scenario analysis

The next step does not treat the causal-discovery output as a uniquely identified directed graph. Instead, it constructs a **theory-augmented working structural causal model (SCM)** for later scenario analysis. This working model is built from three ingredients: first, the robust adjacency backbone identified by the FCI and PC analyses; second, bootstrap evidence on endpoint-mark asymmetry from the pooled FCI extended resamples; and third, a small number of explicitly theory-driven orientation decisions where the bootstrap evidence is weak, symmetric, or in tension with substantive expectations. The resulting graph should therefore be interpreted as a modeling scaffold for simulation rather than as the direct output of the discovery algorithms themselves.

Trimming is used only to reduce the graph to a more manageable skeleton for simulation. In the code, trimming is based on the pooled FCI extended bootstrap: edges are retained when the average no-edge proportion across the two endpoints is below `0.30`. One explicit exception is then added manually, namely the `social_norms – climate_behavior` link, even though its stability is weaker than the rest of the retained skeleton. Orientation is then assigned in graded fashion. Some directions are strongly supported by bootstrap asymmetry, some are supported jointly by bootstrap and theory, and a final subset is imposed mainly on theoretical grounds. This distinction matters, because the evidential status of the edges is not uniform.

::: callout-note
## Trimming and orientation strategy

**Trimming**: retain only edges where the average N-proportion across both endpoints is \< 0.30 in the pooled FCI extended bootstrap.

**Orientation**: for each retained edge, the arrowhead proportion at each endpoint is read from the pooled FCI extended matrix, and the difference between destination and source arrowhead proportions is used as a descriptive measure of directional asymmetry. Larger positive asymmetry is treated as stronger bootstrap support for the stated direction, whereas smaller or conflicting asymmetry indicates that the direction is more assumption-dependent. Final orientation decisions combine this bootstrap evidence with substantive considerations, and the resulting evidential status is documented edge by edge in the orientation table rather than assigned by a fully mechanical cutoff rule.

**`climate_behavior`** is always downstream — background knowledge applied in Section 7.4 prevents it from being oriented as a cause of attitude nodes.

**Sample note.** All path coefficients and residual variances in the working SCM are estimated on the wave-5 subsample (N = 870). Whether these completers differ systematically from the 1,117 participants who did not complete wave 5 is unknown; intervention simulation results should be interpreted with that potential selection bias in mind.
:::

```{r trimmed-setup}
# ── Load extended bootstrap objects ──────────────────────────────────────────
if (!exists("node_order_ext")) {
  node_order_ext <- c(node_order_cd, "climate_behavior")
  p_ext          <- length(node_order_ext)
}

if (!exists("fci_props_ext")) {
  if (!file.exists("pipeline_outputs/fci_props_ext.rds"))
    stop("fci_props_ext.rds not found. Re-render Section 7.4 first.")
  fci_props_ext <- readRDS("pipeline_outputs/fci_props_ext.rds")
  pc_props_ext  <- readRDS("pipeline_outputs/pc_props_ext.rds")
  cat("Loaded fci_props_ext from disk.\n")
} else {
  cat("fci_props_ext already in environment.\n")
```

```{r trimmed-filter}
# ── Step 1: compute average N-proportion for every pair ──────────────────────
n_pair <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = p_ext, ncol = p_ext,
                 dimnames = list(node_order_ext, node_order_ext))

for (i in seq_len(p_ext - 1)) {
  for (j in (i + 1):p_ext) {
    avg_n        <- (fci_props_ext[i, j, "N"] + fci_props_ext[j, i, "N"]) / 2
    n_pair[i, j] <- avg_n
    n_pair[j, i] <- avg_n
  }
}

# ── Step 2: apply N < 0.30 filter ────────────────────────────────────────────
kept_pairs <- list()
for (i in seq_len(p_ext - 1)) {
  for (j in (i + 1):p_ext) {
    if (is.na(n_pair[i, j])) next
    if (n_pair[i, j] < 0.30) {
      kept_pairs[[length(kept_pairs) + 1]] <- data.frame(
        node_i = node_order_ext[i],
        node_j = node_order_ext[j],
        avg_N  = round(n_pair[i, j], 3),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    }
  }
}

# Add SN-CB manually (N = 0.45, theory exception)
kept_pairs[[length(kept_pairs) + 1]] <- data.frame(
  node_i = "social_norms",
  node_j = "climate_behavior",
  avg_N  = 0.45,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

kept_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(kept_pairs)
cat("Retained edges (including SN-CB exception):", nrow(kept_df), "\n\n")

# ── Step 3: print bootstrap arrowhead evidence for each pair ─────────────────
cat(sprintf("%-34s  arr->j  arr->i  asymm   avg_N\n", "Pair"))
cat(strrep("-", 70), "\n")
for (k in seq_len(nrow(kept_df))) {
  ni    <- kept_df$node_i[k]
  nj    <- kept_df$node_j[k]
  i_idx <- which(node_order_ext == ni)
  j_idx <- which(node_order_ext == nj)
  a_j   <- round(fci_props_ext[i_idx, j_idx, ">"], 3)
  a_i   <- round(fci_props_ext[j_idx, i_idx, ">"], 3)
  cat(sprintf("%-34s  %6.3f  %6.3f  %+.3f  %5.3f\n",
              paste(ni, "--", nj), a_j, a_i, a_j - a_i, kept_df$avg_N[k]))
}
```

```{r trimmed-build}
# ── Step 4: build oriented adjacency matrix ───────────────────────────────────
#
# Orientation decisions — documented edge by edge:
#
# NOTE (2026-09-05): the asymm/arr@ numbers transcribed into the comments
# below were read off the Step 3 table when it was still running on the
# N=1000-per-alpha bootstrap. n_boot was since bumped to 2500 per alpha
# (Section 7.3) and the bootstrap was rerun, so fci_props_ext (and the
# Step 3 table above) now reflect N=2500 -- these specific decimal values
# are stale and should be re-read off a fresh Step 3 printout before
# trusting them for anything more precise than "which bucket is this
# edge in." The bucket assignments themselves are unlikely to change
# (these are mostly large-margin asymmetries), but don't quote the exact
# numbers below in the manuscript without checking them again.
#
# STRONG BOOTSTRAP (asymmetry > 0.50 — data unambiguous)
# -------------------------------------------------------
# HF → HP   asymm +0.79  arr@HP=0.85, arr@HF=0.06
#   Future harm is upstream of present harm. Directed in attitude-only FCI.
#   Theoretically: expectations about worsening harm shape perceived current harm.
#
# HP → CB   asymm +0.90  arr@CB=0.96, arr@HP=0.06
#   Present harm drives climate behavior. Strongest CB link in FCI extended.
#
# WR → CB   asymm +1.00  arr@CB=1.00, arr@WR=0.00
#   Weather risk (worry) drives climate behavior. Perfect bootstrap signal.
#
# TS → SN   asymm +0.89  arr@SN=0.94, arr@TS=0.05
#   Trust in science/expert guidance shapes social norms.
#
# POL → PS  asymm +0.84  arr@PS=0.89, arr@POL=0.05
#   Political ideology is upstream of policy support. Unambiguous.
#
# BOOTSTRAP + THEORY (asymmetry 0.15-0.50, both agree)
# -----------------------------------------------------
# BC → TS   asymm +0.43  arr@TS=0.71, arr@BC=0.28
#   Believing climate change is happening precedes trust in scientific guidance.
#   Science-communication literature: belief acceptance → science deference.
#
# BC → PS   asymm +0.45  arr@PS=0.50, arr@BC=0.05
#   Climate belief precedes policy support. Very low absent rate (N=0.05).
#
# BC → HF   asymm +0.25  arr@HF=0.72, arr@BC=0.47
#   General climate belief/concern shapes future harm perceptions.
#
# HP → WR   asymm +0.41  arr@WR=0.69, arr@HP=0.28
#   Perceiving current harm drives weather risk awareness.
#   PC also supports this direction.
#
# BC → HP   asymm +0.18  arr@HP=0.59, arr@BC=0.41
#   Weakest asymmetry in this group, but direction consistent with theory
#   (belief/concern shapes harm perception, not the reverse).
#
# PS → SN   asymm +0.19  arr@SN=0.39, arr@PS=0.20
#   Policy support shapes social norms about lower-carbon behavior.
#
# HF → TS   asymm +0.29 (p_adjacent=0.657 -- closest to the inclusion floor
#   of any retained edge; no established theory story yet for why
#   anticipated future harm would drive trust in expert guidance -- added
#   on the same mechanical-threshold standard as BC->WR below.)
#
# BC → WR   asymm +0.065 (p_adjacent=0.946 -- very robust existence, but
#   the weakest orientation asymmetry of any retained edge; high arrowhead
#   mass at BOTH endpoints, a pattern at least as consistent with a shared
#   latent upstream cause as with a clean direct effect.)
#
# THEORY OVER BOOTSTRAP (bootstrap weak or conflicting)
# -----------------------------------------------------
# TS → PS   asymm +0.40  arr@PS=0.69, arr@TS=0.29
#   Bootstrap slightly favours PS→TS by mark logic (arr@TS=0.89 from PS row)
#   but theory strongly favours TS→PS: deference to scientific expertise is
#   upstream of specific policy endorsement (Druckman & McGrath 2019).
#   Decision: TS → PS, noting the conflict.
#
# POL → BC  asymm +0.33  arr@POL=0.62, arr@BC=0.29
#   Politics is an exogenous background variable. Political identity shapes
#   climate attitudes, not the reverse (Kahan et al. 2012).
#
# SN → CB   asymm +0.49  arr@CB=0.55, arr@SN=0.06  N=0.45 (exception)
#   Retained despite N=0.45. Descriptive norms (perceived social uptake of
#   low-carbon behavior) are established antecedents of individual behavior
#   (Cialdini 2003). Arrowhead asymmetry supports direction.

trimmed_nodes <- node_order_ext
p_tr          <- length(trimmed_nodes)

tr_amat <- matrix(0L, nrow = p_tr, ncol = p_tr,
                  dimnames = list(trimmed_nodes, trimmed_nodes))

add_edge <- function(amat, from, to) {
  amat[from, to] <- 2L
  amat[to, from] <- 3L
  amat
}

# Strong bootstrap
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "harm_future",       "harm_present")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "harm_present",      "climate_behavior")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "weather_risk_prep", "climate_behavior")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "trust_science",     "social_norms")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "politics",          "policy_support")

# Bootstrap + theory
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "belief_concern", "trust_science")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "belief_concern", "policy_support")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "belief_concern", "harm_future")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "harm_present",   "weather_risk_prep")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "belief_concern", "harm_present")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "policy_support", "social_norms")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "harm_future",    "trust_science")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "belief_concern", "weather_risk_prep")

# Theory over bootstrap
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "trust_science",  "policy_support")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "politics",       "belief_concern")
tr_amat <- add_edge(tr_amat, "social_norms",   "climate_behavior")

cat("Total directed edges:", sum(tr_amat == 2L), "\n")

# Topological sort
remaining  <- trimmed_nodes
printed    <- character(0)
topo_order <- character(0)

while (length(remaining) > 0) {
  for (nd in remaining) {
    nd_idx  <- which(trimmed_nodes == nd)
    parents <- trimmed_nodes[sapply(seq_along(trimmed_nodes), function(k) {
      k != nd_idx &&
      tr_amat[k, nd_idx] == 2L &&
      tr_amat[nd_idx, k] == 3L
    })]
    if (all(parents %in% printed)) {
      topo_order <- c(topo_order, nd)
      printed    <- c(printed, nd)
      remaining  <- remaining[remaining != nd]
      break
    }
  }
}

cat("\nDirected edges (topological order):\n")
for (nd in topo_order) {
  nd_idx  <- which(trimmed_nodes == nd)
  parents <- trimmed_nodes[sapply(seq_along(trimmed_nodes), function(k) {
    k != nd_idx &&
    tr_amat[k, nd_idx] == 2L &&
    tr_amat[nd_idx, k] == 3L
  })]
  for (pa in parents) {
    cat(sprintf("  %s -> %s\n", pa, nd))
  }
}
```

```{r trimmed-helpers}
get_parents_tr <- function(node, amat, nms) {
  idx <- which(nms == node)
  nms[sapply(seq_along(nms), function(k) {
    k != idx &&
      amat[k, idx] == 2L &&
      amat[idx, k] == 3L
  })]
}
```

```{r trimmed-orientation-table}
# recover all directed edges from tr_amat
edge_df <- purrr::map_dfr(trimmed_nodes, function(to_node) {
  pa <- get_parents_tr(to_node, tr_amat, trimmed_nodes)
  if (length(pa) == 0) return(NULL)
  tibble::tibble(
    from = as.character(pa),
    to   = as.character(rep(to_node, length(pa)))
  )
})

# pull dimnames once
rn <- dimnames(fci_props_ext)[[1]]
cn <- dimnames(fci_props_ext)[[2]]
mn <- dimnames(fci_props_ext)[[3]]

if (!("N" %in% mn && ">" %in% mn)) {
  stop("fci_props_ext must have mark dimensions including 'N' and '>'")
}

# match edge labels to array indices
edge_stats <- edge_df |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    i_from = match(from, rn),
    i_to   = match(to,   cn)
  )

# stop early with a readable message if anything does not match
bad_idx <- edge_stats |>
  dplyr::filter(is.na(i_from) | is.na(i_to))

if (nrow(bad_idx) > 0) {
  stop(
    "These edge labels were not found in fci_props_ext dimnames:\n",
    paste0(bad_idx$from, " -> ", bad_idx$to, collapse = "\n")
  )
}

# compute numerical summaries using numeric indices
edge_stats <- edge_stats |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    avg_N = purrr::map2_dbl(i_from, i_to,
      ~ (fci_props_ext[.x, .y, "N"] + fci_props_ext[.y, .x, "N"]) / 2),
    arr_to = purrr::map2_dbl(i_from, i_to,
      ~ fci_props_ext[.x, .y, ">"]),
    arr_from = purrr::map2_dbl(i_from, i_to,
      ~ fci_props_ext[.y, .x, ">"]),
    asymm = arr_to - arr_from,
    edge_label = paste0(from, " -> ", to)
  )

# manual interpretation / basis labels
edge_class <- tibble::tribble(
  ~from,               ~to,                 ~Interpretation,                       ~Basis,                                   ~row_group,
  "weather_risk_prep", "climate_behavior",  "Bootstrap clear",                     "FCI bootstrap",                          "FCI bootstrap — unambiguous",
  "harm_present",      "climate_behavior",  "Bootstrap clear",                     "FCI bootstrap",                          "FCI bootstrap — unambiguous",
  "trust_science",     "social_norms",      "Bootstrap clear",                     "FCI bootstrap",                          "FCI bootstrap — unambiguous",
  "politics",          "policy_support",    "Bootstrap clear",                     "FCI bootstrap",                          "FCI bootstrap — unambiguous",
  "harm_future",       "harm_present",      "Bootstrap clear",                     "FCI bootstrap",                          "FCI bootstrap — unambiguous",

  "belief_concern",    "harm_future",       "Bootstrap + theory agree",            "Bootstrap + theory",                     "Bootstrap and theory agree",
  "belief_concern",    "policy_support",    "Bootstrap + theory agree",            "Bootstrap + theory",                     "Bootstrap and theory agree",
  "belief_concern",    "harm_present",      "Bootstrap + theory agree",            "Bootstrap + theory",                     "Bootstrap and theory agree",
  "harm_future",       "trust_science",     "Bootstrap + theory agree (existence near floor)", "Bootstrap + theory",                "Bootstrap and theory agree",
  "belief_concern",    "weather_risk_prep", "Bootstrap + theory agree (weak asymmetry)",        "Bootstrap + theory",                "Bootstrap and theory agree",

  "politics",          "belief_concern",    "Bootstrap favors opposite direction", "Theory (politics exogenous)",            "Theory overrides bootstrap — most assumption-dependent",
  "belief_concern",    "trust_science",     "Bootstrap favors opposite direction", "Theory (belief precedes trust)",         "Theory overrides bootstrap — most assumption-dependent",
  "harm_present",      "weather_risk_prep", "Bootstrap favors opposite direction", "Theory (harm drives risk perception)",      "Theory overrides bootstrap — most assumption-dependent",
  "policy_support",    "social_norms",      "Bootstrap favors opposite direction", "Theory (policy shapes injunctive norm)", "Theory overrides bootstrap — most assumption-dependent",

)
```

## 7.6 Path estimation within the working SCM

Once the working SCM is specified, path estimation is used for two distinct purposes. First, equation-by-equation standardized linear regressions are fit for each endogenous node as local descriptive diagnostics. These regressions are useful for inspecting parent–child relations one equation at a time, but they do not constitute a single jointly estimated system and, in the present implementation, do not all use the same sample. They are therefore reported only as diagnostic summaries.

Second, the full directed system is estimated simultaneously in `lavaan` as a path model on the extended sample (N = 870) using MLR estimation. This simultaneous `lavaan` fit is the basis used to parameterize the SCM for visualization and scenario analysis: both standardized path coefficients and residual variances in the simulation are taken from this same fitted model. These parameters should be interpreted as conditional on the assumed working SCM. They do not validate the graph and should not be read as identified causal effects independent of the structural assumptions introduced in Section 7.5.

The simultaneous `lavaan` model is best understood as a pragmatic approximation for structured scenario analysis rather than as a near-exact representation of the observed covariance structure. Within that qualification, the estimated paths are still informative about the internal logic of the working model. The strongest coefficients lie on the belief–harm–response axis, especially `belief_concern → harm_future`, `belief_concern → trust_science`, and `harm_future → harm_present`. By contrast, the direct paths into `climate_behavior` are more modest: `harm_present` and `weather_risk_prep` are the strongest, whereas `social_norms → climate_behavior` is smaller and more assumption-dependent. This pattern is consistent with the earlier network and causal-discovery results, which also suggested that later behavior is tied most robustly to present-harm salience and weather-related risk perception.

```{r trimmed-sem-weights}

# ── Data ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Attitude-attitude edges: full sample N = 1987
att_nodes_tr <- trimmed_nodes[trimmed_nodes != "climate_behavior"]
att_dat_tr   <- df_main     |> dplyr::select(all_of(att_nodes_tr)) |> as.data.frame()

# CB edges: wave-5 subsample N = 870
ext_dat_tr   <- df_extended |> dplyr::select(all_of(trimmed_nodes)) |> as.data.frame()

# ── Fit one structural equation per non-exogenous node ───────────────────────
sem_rows <- list()

for (nd in trimmed_nodes) {
  pa <- get_parents_tr(nd, tr_amat, trimmed_nodes)
  if (length(pa) == 0) next

  dat_use <- if (nd == "climate_behavior") ext_dat_tr else att_dat_tr
  n_use   <- nrow(dat_use)

  fit <- tryCatch(
    lm(as.formula(paste(nd, "~", paste(pa, collapse = " + "))),
       data = as.data.frame(scale(dat_use))),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) next

  sm    <- summary(fit)
  coefs <- sm$coefficients

  for (parent in pa) {
    sem_rows[[length(sem_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      from  = parent,
      to    = nd,
      beta  = round(coefs[parent, "Estimate"],   3),
      se    = round(coefs[parent, "Std. Error"], 3),
      t_val = round(coefs[parent, "t value"],    3),
      p_val = round(coefs[parent, "Pr(>|t|)"],   4),
      r2    = round(sm$r.squared,                3),
      n     = n_use,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
}

sem_results <- dplyr::bind_rows(sem_rows) |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sig = dplyr::case_when(
      p_val < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_val < 0.01  ~ "**",
      p_val < 0.05  ~ "*",
      TRUE          ~ ""
    ),
    basis = dplyr::case_when(
      paste(from, to) %in% c(
        "harm_future harm_present",
        "harm_present climate_behavior",
        "weather_risk_prep climate_behavior",
        "trust_science social_norms",
        "politics policy_support"
      ) ~ "FCI bootstrap",
      paste(from, to) %in% c(
        "trust_science policy_support",
        "politics belief_concern",
        "social_norms climate_behavior"
      ) ~ "Theory",
      TRUE ~ "Bootstrap + theory"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(factor(to, levels = trimmed_nodes), dplyr::desc(abs(beta)))

cat("Structural equation estimates:\n")
print(sem_results, n = 30)
```

```{r trimmed-lavaan}
# ── Simultaneous SEM via lavaan ───────────────────────────────────────────────
library(lavaan)

lav_lines_tr <- c()
for (nd in trimmed_nodes) {
  pa <- get_parents_tr(nd, tr_amat, trimmed_nodes)
  if (length(pa) == 0) next
  lav_lines_tr <- c(lav_lines_tr,
    paste0(nd, " ~ ", paste(pa, collapse = " + ")))
}
lav_model_tr <- paste(lav_lines_tr, collapse = "\n")

cat("Lavaan model:\n", lav_model_tr, "\n\n")

sem_fit_tr <- lavaan::sem(
  lav_model_tr,
  data      = as.data.frame(scale(ext_dat_tr)),
  estimator = "MLR"
)

cat("=== Global fit ===\n")
print(round(lavaan::fitMeasures(sem_fit_tr,
  c("cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "rmsea.ci.lower",
    "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr", "aic", "bic")), 3))

std_tr <- lavaan::standardizedSolution(sem_fit_tr) |>
  dplyr::filter(op == "~") |>
  dplyr::select(From = rhs, To = lhs,
                Beta = est.std, SE = se, Z = z, p = pvalue) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3)),
    sig = dplyr::case_when(
      p < 0.001 ~ "***", p < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p < 0.05  ~ "*",   TRUE     ~ ""
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(factor(To, levels = trimmed_nodes), dplyr::desc(abs(Beta)))

write.csv(std_tr, "pipeline_outputs/std_path_coefficients_16edge.csv", row.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(
  std_tr,
  caption = paste0(
    "Standardized path coefficients from the simultaneous path model (lavaan, MLR), estimated on the extended sample (N = 870). Fit indices are reported above and suggest that the model is better treated as a working approximation for scenario analysis than as a close-fitting structural representation."
  )
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = TRUE, font_size = 11
  )
```

The simultaneous `lavaan` model provides a useful summary of the implied path structure, but its fit is mixed rather than uniformly strong. Relative fit and residual fit are acceptable to good (`CFI = 0.971`, `TLI = 0.952`, `SRMR = 0.048`), whereas the RMSEA is clearly above conventional close-fit benchmarks (`RMSEA = 0.096`, 90% CI `[0.084, 0.109]`). The model is therefore better understood as a pragmatic approximation for structured scenario analysis than as a near-exact representation of the observed covariance structure. This caution is especially important because the simultaneous path model is estimated on the extended wave-5 subsample (`N = 870`), not on the full `N = 1987` attitude sample.

